The law therefore must be read alongside the Bible's own examples of outsiders received by faith.

Camp sanitation laws follow. Even bodily waste must be handled outside the camp because God walks among His people. Holiness is embodied and practical.

A striking law says an escaped slave who has taken refuge in Israel must not be handed back to his master. He may live where he chooses and must not be oppressed. In the ancient Near Eastern world, that is a significant protection for a fugitive.

Israel must not charge interest to a poor fellow Israelite in the ordinary lending situation described here, and vows must be fulfilled. Yet Moses adds that not making a vow is no sin. God does not demand dramatic promises.

Chapter 24 contains the law Jesus later discusses concerning divorce. A man writes a certificate of divorce, and if the woman marries another man she cannot later return to the first husband after the second marriage ends.

The passage regulates an existing practice; it does not command divorce or present it as creation's ideal. Jesus explicitly says Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart and directs attention back to Genesis.

A newly married man is exempt from military duty for a year “to bring joy to the wife he has married.” Domestic care receives protection from public demands.

A millstone may not be taken as collateral because that would seize a person's means of making food. Kidnapping a fellow Israelite for slavery is a capital crime.

Employers must pay poor laborers promptly. Justice must not be denied to resident aliens or fatherless children, and a widow's garment may not be taken as collateral.

Then Moses gives the theological reason: “Remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you from there.”

Harvesters must leave forgotten sheaves, olives, and grapes for resident aliens, fatherless, and widows.

Notice the form of charity. The vulnerable are given access to harvest rather than treated as invisible. Ruth will later live within precisely this kind of gleaning provision.

Again Deuteronomy joins holiness to ordinary economics. How collateral is taken, when wages are paid, what a farmer leaves behind, and how a foreigner is treated are all matters before God.
difficult:
“Assembly of the LORD” is difficult to define precisely, and the restrictions should not be casually equated with exclusion from salvation. Ruth's story is an important canonical check against such a reading.

The fugitive-slave law is notable because many ancient legal systems required return of escaped slaves. It does not abolish every form of ancient servitude, but it clearly protects a runaway from forced return.

Jesus' discussion of Deuteronomy 24 shows that a law can regulate a broken human situation without expressing God's original creational ideal.
connections:
Jesus appeals behind the divorce regulation to Genesis: “from the beginning it was not so.” That teaches Christians to distinguish concession within a fallen society from creation's design.

James' condemnation of withheld wages strongly echoes Deuteronomy's concern for poor workers.

Ruth's gleaning in Boaz's field gives narrative flesh to these laws. God's care for the outsider and widow is mediated through ordinary obedience and generosity.

title: Fairness, Firstfruits, and the Story Israel Confesses
explanation:
Deuteronomy 25 continues with case laws aimed at proportional justice. When corporal punishment is ordered, lashes are capped at forty “so that your brother is not degraded in your sight.” Even a guilty person retains human dignity.

“You must not muzzle an ox while it treads out grain” protects a working animal's access to food. Paul later applies the principle analogically to support for gospel workers: if even an animal should share in the fruit of its labor, human workers certainly should.

The levirate-marriage law addresses a man who dies without a son. His brother is expected to marry the widow so that the dead brother's family line and inheritance continue. If the brother refuses, there is a public procedure of shame, but the widow cannot simply seize him privately.

The strange case of a woman grabbing a man's genitals during a fight reflects concern for reproductive injury and family continuity. The prescribed punishment is unusually severe and translations differ in how literally to understand “cut off her hand.” It is one of the Torah's difficult legal cases and should not be generalized into modern criminal sentencing.

Honest weights and measures follow. Economic fraud is not a minor business tactic; it is detestable to God.

The chapter closes by commanding Israel to remember Amalek's attack on the weak and stragglers during the Exodus and eventually blot out Amalek's memory. The severity belongs to the larger conquest/judgment setting and will become important in 1 Samuel.

Chapter 26 shifts from case law to liturgy. When Israel settles the land, the worshiper brings firstfruits and recites a compact confession of salvation history:

“My father was a wandering Aramean... the Egyptians mistreated us... we cried out... the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand... he brought us to this place and gave us this land.”

Israel's creed is a story of grace.

The firstfruits are therefore not payment to persuade God to bless them. They are response to a land already given.

The worshiper then rejoices with Levites and resident aliens.

A separate declaration accompanies the third-year tithe, which supports Levites, resident aliens, fatherless, and widows. Worship and social care again belong together.

The chapter concludes with mutual covenant language: Israel has affirmed that the LORD is their God, and the LORD has affirmed Israel as His treasured people.

But the order throughout Deuteronomy remains decisive. Israel did not rescue itself and then enter a contract with God as equal partners. God heard, rescued, carried, gave, and chose. Israel's confession and obedience answer His prior action.

The firstfruits basket therefore becomes a small sermon: “I am here because God kept His promise.”
difficult:
The levirate law addresses inheritance and protection of a widow within ancient clan structures; it is not a Christian command that widows marry a deceased husband's brother.

The corporal-punishment and unusual injury laws belong to Israel's civil code, not church discipline.

The Amalek command is a specific divine judgment in Israel's history. It cannot authorize ethnic hatred or modern religious violence.
connections:
Paul quotes the unmuzzled-ox command in both 1 Corinthians and 1 Timothy to defend material support for those who labor in ministry.

The firstfruits confession models how biblical faith remembers salvation: identity is narrated from God's acts rather than human achievement.

Christians similarly confess a saving history they did not accomplish—Christ died, Christ rose, God baptized and called us through the gospel—and then offer lives of thanksgiving because salvation has already been given.

title: Mount Ebal, Blessing, Curse, and the Terrible Cost of Covenant Rebellion
explanation:
As Israel prepares to cross the Jordan, Moses commands a covenant ceremony in the land. Large stones coated with plaster are to bear the words of the law, and an altar of uncut stones is to be built on Mount Ebal.

Half the tribes will stand on Mount Gerizim for blessing and half on Mount Ebal for curse. The Levites announce curses against hidden or destructive sins, and the people answer, “Amen.”

The list is revealing: secret idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving boundary markers, misleading the blind, denying justice to vulnerable people, sexual violations, secret murder, bribery, and failure to uphold the law.

Some are crimes a person might imagine escaping because no human authority sees them. The covenant ceremony teaches that Israel lives before God.

Chapter 28 expands the blessings and curses dramatically.

If Israel faithfully obeys, covenant blessing reaches city and field, children and crops, baskets and livestock, travel and national security. These are concrete land-covenant blessings for Israel.

The curse section is much longer. Disease, drought, crop failure, military defeat, oppression, madness, loss of family and property, siege, and exile unfold with increasing horror.

The siege descriptions include cannibalism—a terrible reality later associated with ancient warfare and, tragically, with Jerusalem's judgment. The text does not command such behavior; it warns what social collapse under siege can become.

The climax is exile. Israel, rescued from Egypt, will experience a dreadful reversal and be scattered among nations.

Why so severe? Because the covenant is not a casual arrangement. Israel has received extraordinary privilege: God's presence, law, land, and promise. Persistent idolatry repudiates the God who redeemed them.

Yet Christians must resist turning Deuteronomy 28 into a simple formula for individual life. A Christian with cancer is not under Deuteronomy's curse because of inadequate faith. A wealthy person is not thereby proven obedient. These sanctions concern Israel as the Sinai covenant nation in its land.

Indeed, the later Old Testament uses this chapter to interpret Israel's national history. Kings and prophets will describe drought, invasion, and exile in covenantal terms.

Deuteronomy 28 also creates a theological crisis that the rest of Scripture must answer. Israel will in fact break the covenant. If blessing depends on perfect covenant faithfulness, who can stand?

The answer will eventually lead beyond Israel's obedience to the faithful Messiah who bears the curse for His people.
difficult:
The blessings and curses are specifically Mosaic-covenant sanctions. They should not be preached as a prosperity contract for Christians.

The horrific siege language describes consequences of warfare and judgment, not divine approval of cannibalism or atrocity.

Verse 68's reference to return toward Egypt is a covenant-reversal image; it need not require that every exile literally terminate in Egypt.
connections:
Galatians 3 quotes Deuteronomy's curse language: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue doing everything written in the book of the law.” Paul then announces the gospel: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”

That is not God deciding the law never mattered. Christ bears the judgment sin deserves.

The public “Amen” also reminds us that the law exposes rather than flatters us. Its final Christian use drives us away from self-righteousness and toward the One who fulfilled righteousness and bore the curse.

title: The Hidden Things, the Revealed Word, and a Circumcised Heart
explanation:
Moses renews the covenant with Israel on the plains of Moab. Those standing before him include leaders, children, women, resident aliens, and laborers—but the covenant also reaches “those who are not here with us today,” future generations who belong to Israel's continuing story.

Moses warns against the person who hears the covenant curse yet privately says, “I will have peace even though I follow my own stubborn heart.” Membership in the community is not a magical shield against unbelief.

Future generations and foreigners will see the devastated land and ask why this happened. The answer: Israel abandoned the covenant and served other gods.

Then comes the often-quoted line: “The hidden things belong to the LORD our God, but the revealed things belong to us and our children forever, so that we may follow all the words of this law.”

The verse is not an excuse to avoid hard thinking. It distinguishes what God has chosen not to reveal from what He has clearly given. Faith does not need secret knowledge in order to obey God's revealed Word.

Chapter 30 astonishingly looks beyond the exile already anticipated. After blessing and curse have come and Israel is scattered, God will gather them again.

Most importantly: “The LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love him with all your heart and all your soul so that you will live.”

Earlier Israel was commanded to circumcise its heart. Now God promises to do it.

That is a crucial biblical movement. The law can name and demand the heart Israel ought to have; God's restoring grace must create the heart that loves Him.

Moses then says the command is not inaccessible—Israel need not ascend to heaven or cross the sea to find it. “The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart.”

The chapter ends with life and death, blessing and curse set before Israel. “Choose life,” Moses says, by loving the LORD, obeying Him, and holding fast to Him, “for he is your life.”

This is covenant exhortation addressed to the redeemed nation, not a philosophical statement that fallen sinners generate saving faith from autonomous free will. Deuteronomy itself has already identified the deeper need: God must circumcise the heart.

The tension between command and promise is important for Lutheran reading. God's law truly commands; human inability does not make the command unreal. But salvation does not finally rest on our ability to manufacture the obedient heart the law requires.

God's promise reaches where command alone cannot.
difficult:
“Choose life” should be read in its covenant context. It is a real summons to Israel, but it does not settle later theological debates by itself about the fallen will's ability to create saving faith.

The promise of heart circumcision is one of Deuteronomy's strongest indications that Israel's fundamental problem cannot be solved merely by receiving more commands.

“The hidden things” does not mean theology should avoid questions Scripture actually addresses. It warns against claiming access to what God has not revealed.
connections:
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30 in Romans 10 and applies its “word is near you” language to the gospel of Christ. We do not climb to heaven to bring Christ down or descend to raise Him; God has acted, and the gospel announces what He has done.

The promise of a changed heart stands alongside Jeremiah's new covenant and Ezekiel's promise of a new heart and Spirit.

This is deeply compatible with Lutheran emphasis: faith and love are not achievements by which we cause grace. God's Word comes near, and God Himself does the heart-changing work His promise describes.

title: Moses' Song: Israel Will Fail, but God Remains Faithful
explanation:
Moses is now 120 years old. He tells Israel that he will not cross the Jordan and publicly commissions Joshua: “Be strong and courageous.”

The encouragement is grounded not in Joshua's personality but God's presence: “The LORD is the one who will go before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or abandon you.”

Moses writes down the law and commands that it be read publicly every seven years during the Festival of Shelters so men, women, children, and resident aliens can hear, learn, fear the LORD, and obey. Israel's covenant life depends on repeated hearing.

Then God tells Moses something sobering: after Moses dies, Israel will turn to other gods and break the covenant.

The law is therefore written not under an illusion that information alone will fix Israel. God knows their future apostasy.

Moses is commanded to teach Israel a song that will serve as a witness. Songs lodge in communal memory in ways prose sometimes does not.

Chapter 32, the Song of Moses, begins by calling heaven and earth as witnesses. God's teaching is compared to rain and dew, and God is proclaimed “the Rock—his work is perfect; all his ways are just.”

The contrast is immediate: God is faithful; His people act corruptly.

Moses recalls God's care for Israel with vivid imagery. God found Jacob in a desolate land, guarded him “as the pupil of his eye,” and cared for him like an eagle hovering over its young.

But prosperity leads to apostasy: “Jeshurun became fat and rebelled.” Israel abandons the Rock who gave birth to them and sacrifices to false gods.

Judgment follows. Yet the song turns again. God will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants when their strength is gone.

The false gods will be exposed as powerless. God alone kills and makes alive, wounds and heals.

The song's ending expands beyond Israel: “Rejoice, you nations, concerning his people,” because God will avenge His servants and make atonement for His land and people.

Moses then tells Israel these words are not empty: “They are your life.”

Finally God tells Moses to ascend Mount Nebo, see the land, and die because of his failure at Meribah.

The great lawgiver reaches the border but cannot complete the journey. His final song has already admitted why a deeper salvation is needed: God's people possess the Word and still rebel.

The hope rests finally in the Rock who remains faithful.
difficult:
Deuteronomy 31's prediction of Israel's apostasy does not make Israel's choices meaningless. Scripture can affirm both divine foreknowledge and genuine human responsibility without explaining the philosophical mechanics.

Some textual traditions of Deuteronomy 32:8 read “sons of God,” while the traditional Hebrew text underlying many translations reads “sons of Israel.” The “sons of God” reading has strong ancient manuscript support and may refer to heavenly beings associated with the nations. The passage remains emphatically monotheistic: the LORD alone is Israel's God.

The eagle imagery is metaphorical divine care, not a scientific description of eagle behavior that must be pressed in every detail.
connections:
Paul quotes portions of the Song of Moses in Romans, and Hebrews echoes its declaration that vengeance belongs to God.

The song's contrast between Israel's unfaithfulness and God's faithfulness reaches its resolution in Christ, the faithful Israelite and Son.

Joshua is told God will not abandon him; Hebrews later applies similar language to believers. Christian courage is likewise grounded not in confidence in ourselves but in God's promise.

title: Moses Dies, but the Promise Goes On
explanation:
Deuteronomy closes with blessing and death.

Before Moses dies, he blesses Israel tribe by tribe. The form recalls Jacob's blessings in Genesis 49, placing Moses at the end of another major stage in Israel's story.

The poem begins with God appearing from Sinai in majesty, accompanied by holy ones, and giving instruction to Israel. The tribal blessings then speak of survival, strength, land, priestly service, security, and God's help.

Levi receives special attention for teaching God's ordinances and offering worship. Joseph receives rich agricultural blessing. Asher is pictured with abundance and security.

The closing lines turn from individual tribes to Israel as a whole: “There is none like the God of Jeshurun, who rides the heavens to your aid.”

“The God of old is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms.”

Israel's security ultimately rests not in the land, armies, or Moses but in God Himself.

Chapter 34 then narrates Moses' death.

He climbs Mount Nebo, and God shows him the land from Gilead through the Jordan valley. Moses sees what was promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob but does not enter it.

He dies in Moab at 120 years old. The text says his eyesight was not weak and his vitality had not left him, emphasizing that his death is not presented simply as physical decline.

God buries Moses, and no one knows his grave. That mysterious detail prevents the story from becoming a shrine narrative centered on Moses' tomb.

Israel mourns thirty days. Joshua is full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses laid hands on him, and Israel begins listening to its new leader.

Yet the book ends by looking backward at Moses: “No prophet has arisen again in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face.”

That statement creates expectation.

Deuteronomy 18 promised that God would raise up a prophet like Moses. Deuteronomy 34 says Israel has not yet seen one.

Joshua is Moses' legitimate successor, but he is not Moses' equal. The prophetic story remains open.

Moses' greatness lies in his unique relationship with God and in the signs performed through him in Egypt. Yet even Moses is a servant who sins, dies, and cannot bring Israel into the land.

That does not diminish him. It clarifies his place. He is the great old-covenant mediator whose ministry points beyond itself.

The Torah therefore ends with both fulfillment and incompleteness. Israel has been redeemed from Egypt, received God's covenant, survived the wilderness, and stands ready for Canaan. But sin remains. Moses is dead. The promised prophet is still awaited. The lasting rest is still ahead.

God's promise, however, has not died with Moses.

The next book begins with precisely that fact: “After the death of Moses the LORD's servant, the LORD spoke to Joshua.”

Servants pass away. God's Word and promise continue.
difficult:
Moses' authorship of Deuteronomy does not require him to have written the account of his own death. The final chapter naturally reads as an inspired concluding notice added after his death, whether by Joshua or another authorized hand; Scripture does not identify the human writer.

“No prophet has arisen like Moses” likely reflects a vantage point after Moses and intentionally complements the promise of Deuteronomy 18.

The location of Moses' grave is explicitly unknown. Later traditions claiming certainty about it go beyond the biblical text.
connections:
The New Testament identifies Jesus as the long-awaited prophet like Moses, while also presenting Him as far greater than Moses.

Hebrews says Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house.

Moses sees the inheritance but cannot bring Israel into it. Joshua will bring Israel into Canaan, yet Hebrews says even Joshua did not provide God's final rest. The Torah's unfinished hope ultimately reaches beyond both men to Christ.

title: Be Strong and Courageous: God Keeps His Promise
explanation:
Joshua begins with blunt words: “Moses my servant is dead.” Israel has lost the great leader who confronted Pharaoh, received the law, spoke with God, and led the people for forty years. Yet God's promise has not died with Moses.

God tells Joshua to cross the Jordan with the people and enter the land promised to their ancestors. Joshua's courage is therefore not positive thinking. Four times the chapter emphasizes strength and courage, but the reason is always outside Joshua himself: God has promised the land, God will be with him, and God will not abandon him.

Joshua's responsibility is to act according to God's Word. He must carefully observe the instruction Moses gave, not turning from it right or left. “This book of instruction must not depart from your mouth; you are to meditate on it day and night.” Biblical meditation here is not emptying the mind but filling speech, thought, and action with God's revealed Word.

The promise that Joshua will “prosper and succeed” must be read in that covenant setting. This is not a general guarantee that Bible reading produces financial success. Joshua has been commissioned for a particular task in God's promise to Israel.

Joshua then commands the officers to prepare the people. Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh are reminded of their agreement with Moses: their families may remain east of the Jordan, but their warriors must help the other tribes receive their inheritance. They affirm Joshua's leadership and echo God's command: “Above all, be strong and courageous!”

Chapter 2 shifts to Jericho. Joshua secretly sends two spies, who enter the house of Rahab, a prostitute. The king of Jericho hears of them, but Rahab hides them and misdirects the king's men.

Rahab's confession is remarkable. She has heard what the LORD did at the Red Sea and to the Amorite kings. “The LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth below.”

Israel itself repeatedly saw God's works and responded with unbelief. Rahab, a Canaanite outsider with only reports of those works, confesses Israel's God.

She asks that her family be spared. The spies swear to protect everyone gathered in her house, provided she marks the window with a scarlet cord and keeps their mission secret.

Rahab's lie to the king raises a genuine ethical question. The narrative clearly praises her reception and protection of the spies and later Scripture commends her faith. It does not pause to give a general doctrine of lying. Christian interpreters have disagreed over whether deception is permissible to protect innocent life under murderous regimes. We should distinguish the text's clear commendation of Rahab's faith from conclusions it does not explicitly draw about every feature of her action.

The spies return with an extraordinary report: “The LORD has handed over the entire land to us.” Forty years earlier, ten spies saw Canaan's strength and concluded Israel could not enter. Now two spies hear from a Canaanite woman that the inhabitants themselves are melting in fear.

Joshua begins with succession, but its deeper subject is God's continuity. Moses dies. Joshua leads. Rahab is unexpectedly gathered into the promise. Through every change, God remains faithful to His Word.
difficult:
The conquest begins in these chapters and will become morally difficult. Joshua presents it as a unique divine judgment and fulfillment of the land promise, not as a timeless right for God's people to conquer territory.

Rahab is explicitly called a prostitute. Scripture neither hides her past nor makes it the last word about her. Her confession and actions identify her with Israel's God.

The scarlet cord is a practical sign agreed upon by Rahab and the spies. Christian preaching has sometimes made its color a direct symbol of Christ's blood. That can become imaginative allegory; Joshua itself does not make that connection.
connections:
Hebrews 13 echoes God's promise to Joshua—“I will never leave you or abandon you”—and applies God's faithful presence to believers.

Hebrews 11 and James 2 both remember Rahab as an example of faith expressed in action. Matthew includes Rahab in Jesus' genealogy. The Canaanite prostitute becomes an ancestor in the Messiah's human line.

Joshua's name is the Hebrew form corresponding to Jesus—“The LORD saves.” Joshua will lead Israel into an earthly inheritance, but Hebrews later says that Joshua did not give God's people their final rest. The greater Joshua does.

title: Through the Jordan into the Promised Land
explanation:
Israel now stands at the Jordan during flood stage. The river is not merely a geographical boundary; crossing it marks the end of wilderness wandering and entrance into the promised land.

The ark of the covenant goes ahead. Israel is told to keep its distance because the ark represents God's holy presence. Joshua says, “Consecrate yourselves, because the LORD will do wonders among you tomorrow.”

When the priests carrying the ark step into the water, the river stops upstream and the people cross on dry ground. The language deliberately recalls the Red Sea. God is establishing Joshua's leadership in continuity with Moses, but more importantly He is showing the new generation that the God who brought Israel out of Egypt is bringing Israel into Canaan.

The priests remain standing in the middle of the dry riverbed until everyone has crossed.

Chapter 4 turns the miracle into memory. One man from each tribe takes a stone from the Jordan and a memorial is established at Gilgal. Moses repeatedly commanded parents to teach children the meaning of God's acts; now Joshua does the same.

“When your children ask their fathers in the future, ‘What is the meaning of these stones?’” Israel must tell the story.

The stones are not magical. They are prompts for proclamation. Their purpose is that Israel's children and “all the peoples of the earth” may know the LORD's hand is strong.

Chapter 5 shows the theological preparation required before military action. The new generation is circumcised because those born during the wilderness years had not received the covenant sign. Israel then celebrates Passover.

The order matters. Before Jericho falls, Israel is marked by covenant and fed by remembrance of redemption.

The day after they eat produce from Canaan, the manna stops. God's provision changes because Israel's circumstances have changed. The ending of manna is not abandonment; it is fulfillment. They now eat from the land toward which manna sustained them.

Then Joshua encounters a mysterious figure with a drawn sword, “the commander of the LORD's army.” Joshua asks the natural wartime question: “Are you for us or for our enemies?”

The answer is startling: “Neither.”

Joshua's question assumes God's commander can be fitted into Israel's side of the conflict. The encounter reverses the perspective. The real issue is not whether God joins Joshua's cause but whether Joshua stands under God's command.

Joshua falls facedown. He is told, as Moses was at the burning bush, “Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy.”

The parallel suggests an extraordinary manifestation of God's holy presence. Interpreters disagree whether this figure is an angelic commander or a visible manifestation of the LORD Himself. The text creates a close association without explaining the figure's identity in later theological categories.

Israel has crossed the river, but the final scene prevents triumphalism. The land is God's gift, the battle is God's, and Joshua himself must bow.
difficult:
The Jordan miracle is presented as a real divine act deliberately paralleling the Red Sea. Attempts to explain it solely through natural river blockage miss the narrator's emphasis, though God can of course use natural means in providence.

Circumcision's apparent neglect during the wilderness years is stated but not fully explained. The text emphasizes restoring covenant practice before conquest.

The commander's “Neither” does not mean God is neutral about everything in the coming conflict. God has commanded Israel to enter the land. It rebukes the assumption that God is simply a tribal asset under Israel's control.
connections:
Baptismal theology has long drawn on Israel passing through water into a new life under God's promise, though the New Testament more explicitly connects baptism with the Red Sea in 1 Corinthians 10 and with Christ's death and resurrection in Romans 6.

The memorial stones illustrate how faith is transmitted: God's saving acts are remembered and spoken to the next generation.

The holy-ground encounter recalls Moses and points to a central biblical truth: leaders of God's people remain servants under God's Word. No office places Joshua—or any later leader—above the Holy One.

title: Jericho Falls—and Israel Discovers the Enemy Within
explanation:
Jericho is tightly shut because of Israel, but Israel does not capture it by conventional siege tactics.

God commands the army to march around the city once each day for six days with priests, trumpets, and the ark. On the seventh day they circle seven times, the priests blow the trumpets, the people shout, and the wall collapses.

The strange strategy makes the theological claim unmistakable: Jericho is given by God. Israel cannot reasonably credit superior siege engineering.

The city is placed under *herem*, often translated “devoted to destruction.” Everything is placed under God's judgment except Rahab and those gathered in her house. Silver, gold, bronze, and iron are placed in the LORD's treasury rather than taken as ordinary plunder.

This is one of Scripture's hard conquest texts. Joshua presents Jericho's destruction as divine judgment, not ethnic hatred or permission for later religious conquest. The Canaanite Rahab is spared and incorporated into Israel precisely because the dividing line is not simple ethnicity.

The moral difficulty remains real. The text describes comprehensive destruction, and readers should not pretend that language is emotionally easy. Biblical theology locates this event within a unique period of judgment and promise; Christians have no mandate to reenact it.

After Jericho's victory, chapter 7 delivers a shock. Israel attacks the much smaller town of Ai and is defeated. About thirty-six Israelites die.

Joshua tears his clothes and laments before God. His prayer begins sounding disturbingly like the wilderness generation: why did you bring us across the Jordan only to destroy us?

God tells him to get up. The problem is not God's faithfulness. “Israel has sinned.”

Achan has secretly taken items from Jericho that were devoted to God—a beautiful Babylonian garment, silver, and gold—and hidden them beneath his tent.

The sin of one man is described corporately: “Israel has sinned.” Ancient Israel's covenant identity is far more communal than modern Western individualism. Achan's hidden act compromises the community.

The process of identifying Achan moves from tribe to clan to household to individual. He confesses: “I saw... I coveted... and took.” The sequence echoes the basic pattern of temptation: sight, desire, seizure.

Achan, his property, and apparently members of his household are destroyed. The account is severe, particularly regarding the household. The text does not tell us the degree to which family members knew of goods hidden under the family tent, so claims of either complete innocence or proven complicity go beyond what is stated.

The contrast between Rahab and Achan is striking. Rahab is a Canaanite outsider who trusts Israel's God and is brought in. Achan is an Israelite insider who treats what belongs to God as his own and is cast out.

Joshua therefore refuses an ethnic or merely external definition of holiness. Being physically inside Israel is not a shield against unbelief.

The first two battles teach complementary lessons: Israel cannot win because it is strong, and Israel cannot presume on God's presence while despising His Word.
difficult:
The extent and archaeological dating of Jericho's destruction are debated. Archaeological reconstructions depend heavily on dating pottery and destruction layers, and scholars do not agree on how those findings correlate with biblical chronology. The theological reading should not rest on overstating archaeological certainty.

*Herem* language can denote placing persons or things irrevocably under God's claim, often through destruction. Its conquest use is unique and must not be transferred to Christian mission.

Achan's household is a difficult feature. The text does not explicitly describe their knowledge, though the hidden goods were under the tent. We should acknowledge the difficulty rather than invent details.
connections:
Hebrews 11 says Jericho's walls fell “by faith” after Israel marched seven days, and immediately names Rahab as one who did not perish with the disobedient.

Achan's “saw, coveted, took” pattern resembles Genesis 3 and later biblical descriptions of desire giving birth to sin.

Most importantly, these chapters undermine religious presumption. God's gifts are received by faith; membership, success, or past victories do not make God controllable.

title: Renewal at Ebal, the Gibeonites, and the Long Day
explanation:
After Achan's sin has been exposed and judged, God begins chapter 8 with words Joshua badly needs: “Do not be afraid or discouraged.” The defeat at Ai was real, but it did not mean God's promise had failed. Israel is sent back to the city, this time with an ambush strategy.

There is an important contrast with Jericho. At Jericho the spoil was devoted to God and Israel could take none of it. At Ai God explicitly permits the people to keep livestock and plunder. That makes Achan's grasping especially tragic: he seized what God had forbidden when God was perfectly able to give in His own time.

After the victory Joshua does something that might seem strategically odd: he takes Israel to Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim to carry out Moses' instructions from Deuteronomy 27. He builds an altar, offers sacrifices, writes the law on stones, and reads the blessings and curses before the whole assembly—men, women, children, and resident aliens.

The placement is theological. Israel's victories do not put Israel above God's Word. Before the conquest proceeds, the conquerors themselves stand under the law that blesses faithfulness and condemns rebellion.

Chapter 9 then shows how quickly success can produce vulnerability. The Gibeonites know Israel's victories and devise a deception. They arrive with worn-out sacks, cracked wineskins, old sandals, and dry bread, claiming to have traveled from a distant land.

The key sentence is easy to miss: Israel's leaders examined their provisions “but did not seek the LORD's decision.”

Their mistake is not that they failed to be suspicious enough. They trusted what looked obvious without seeking the guidance God had provided Israel. Joshua makes a treaty, and three days later they discover that Gibeon is nearby.

Israel nevertheless keeps the oath. The Gibeonites become servants associated with the sanctuary. Later Scripture treats that oath as binding; Saul's attempt to violate it brings bloodguilt in 2 Samuel 21.

The story is also another crack in any simplistic ethnic reading of the conquest. Rahab, a Canaanite, has already been spared and incorporated into Israel. Now an entire Canaanite community survives because it seeks peace with Israel's God and people, even though it does so deceptively.

Chapter 10 follows directly from that treaty. Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon because it has made peace with Israel. Joshua marches all night to defend his new allies.

God throws the enemy into confusion and sends hailstones. Then comes the famous command: “Sun, stand still over Gibeon, and moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.”

The text says daylight was extraordinarily prolonged until Israel prevailed and concludes, “There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD listened to a man, because the LORD fought for Israel.”

The text does not explain the physical mechanism. The language is ordinary observational language—the same kind by which we still speak of sunrise and sunset. Proposals involving slowed rotation, unusual refraction, an eclipse, or poetic battle language have all been offered, but none can be established from the passage. The narrator's claim is theological and historical: God intervened extraordinarily for Israel.

The chapter then describes a sweeping southern campaign. Its violence remains difficult. Joshua presents these events as particular divine judgment in the unique conquest of Canaan, not as a pattern for Christians to imitate.

The church's mission is not to take land from unbelievers. Christ sends His church with Word and sacrament, making disciples rather than waging holy war.
difficult:
Joshua 10:12–14 is one of the Bible's most debated miracle texts. We should affirm what the text actually says—that God extraordinarily gave Israel the time needed for victory—without pretending Scripture tells us exactly what happened astronomically.

The Gibeonite story does not make deception a virtue. Its clearest lesson is Israel's failure to consult God and the seriousness of an oath once made.

The conquest language is severe. It belongs to a bounded act of judgment connected with the land promise. It cannot be transferred to modern ethnic conflict, nationalism, or Christian mission.
connections:
The Ebal ceremony shows the law judging Israel as well as Canaan. God's people never become righteous simply by being on the “right side” historically.

The Gibeonites join Rahab as outsiders unexpectedly preserved among God's covenant people, anticipating the widening biblical story in which the nations receive blessing through Abraham's offspring.

Most importantly, “the LORD fought for Israel” keeps Israel from boasting. Victory is gift. For Christians, final victory likewise belongs to God, but it comes climactically through the crucified and risen Christ.

title: Victory in the North and a Record of God's Faithfulness
explanation:
After the southern campaign, chapter 11 describes an even larger threat. Jabin king of Hazor gathers northern kings and an army “as numerous as the sand on the seashore,” with many horses and chariots.

From Israel's perspective this is overwhelming military power. God again tells Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them.” The reason is not that Joshua has secretly become stronger than they are. God promises to give them into Israel's hand.

Joshua attacks suddenly at the waters of Merom. The coalition collapses, and Hazor—the leading city of the alliance—is burned.

God tells Joshua to hamstring the captured horses and burn the chariots. In the ancient world, chariots were elite military technology. Israel is not being trained to build its security around the same military machinery on which Canaanite kings relied. Later Deuteronomy's warning that Israel's king must not multiply horses makes the theological issue clearer: Israel's confidence is to rest in the LORD.

The chapter contains sweeping statements: Joshua took “the entire land,” destroyed the enemy, and left no survivors in the areas described. Yet the same book has already said much land remains, and later chapters repeatedly mention Canaanites still living among Israel.

Joshua itself therefore teaches us how to hear its conquest rhetoric. These are ancient victory summaries describing decisive defeat of organized resistance, not necessarily a claim that every Canaanite individual in every settlement has vanished. That observation does not remove the violence, but it prevents us from forcing the text into a more absolute claim than the book itself sustains.

Verse 20 says the LORD hardened the Canaanites' hearts so they would meet Israel in battle and come under judgment. This resembles Pharaoh in Exodus.

Divine hardening is difficult because Scripture holds together two truths modern readers often want separated: these rulers genuinely oppose God, and God sovereignly uses even their resistance within His judgment. The text does not portray morally innocent people who wanted peace being forced by God to become evil. Rahab and Gibeon have already shown that Canaanites who seek refuge are not mechanically destroyed because of ethnicity.

The Anakim are also defeated. These were the giants whose presence had terrified the spies forty years earlier. The obstacle that once became the excuse for unbelief is now overcome.

Then “the land had rest from war.”

Chapter 12 is essentially a victory register. It first names Sihon and Og, defeated under Moses east of the Jordan, and then lists thirty-one kings defeated under Joshua west of the Jordan.

Lists of unfamiliar names can feel like dead space in Bible reading. Here the list functions almost like a row of memorial stones. Each name represents a place where Israel once faced an enemy and where God's promise proved dependable.

The chapter also connects Moses and Joshua. The conquest is not Joshua's independent achievement. What began under Moses continues under Joshua because the same God is keeping the same promise.

Joshua 11–12 therefore marks a major turning point. The great coalitions have been broken. Israel has not yet settled every portion of land, but the decisive phase of conquest is complete.

The narrator wants the reader to see more than military history: the God who promised the land to Abraham has not forgotten what He said centuries earlier.
difficult:
The conquest summaries should be read alongside later statements about remaining Canaanites. Ancient war accounts often use comprehensive language for decisive victory. Joshua's own narrative makes clear that settlement remained incomplete.

Divine hardening does not erase human responsibility. Scripture affirms God's sovereignty and the rulers' real hostility without giving us a philosophical formula that explains every aspect of their relationship.

The destruction of Canaan remains morally difficult. The text presents it as God's particular judgment, not Israelite racial superiority and not authorization for later religious conquest.
connections:
Hebrews later looks back on Canaan's “rest” and says it was not God's final rest. Joshua's achievement is real but provisional.

The list of defeated kings is a reminder that biblical faith is rooted in God's acts in history, not vague optimism.

Christians do not reproduce Joshua's wars. The New Testament locates our struggle against sin, death, the devil, and spiritual evil, while Christ's kingdom advances through the gospel rather than territorial conquest.

title: The Land Is Given—and Much Remains
explanation:
Joshua 13 opens with an apparent tension: Joshua is old, and God says, “A great deal of the land remains to be possessed.”

That matters because earlier chapters spoke of Joshua taking the whole land. The book itself does not see a contradiction. Israel has decisively broken organized Canaanite resistance, but actual settlement and possession remain incomplete.

God lists unconquered territories and promises, “I will drive them out before the Israelites.” Joshua's task now shifts toward allotting inheritance.

The eastern territories previously given to Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh are reviewed. Levi receives no territorial inheritance because “the offerings made by fire to the LORD” and ultimately the LORD Himself are their inheritance.

The repeated word “inheritance” is important. The land is not merely booty Israel has earned through military success. It is a gift apportioned under God's promise.

Chapter 14 introduces Caleb. Forty-five years have passed since he explored Canaan. At eighty-five he asks for the hill country promised to him.

Caleb says, “I followed the LORD my God completely.” This is not a claim of sinless perfection. It refers particularly to his faithful response when the other spies discouraged Israel.

He asks for Hebron, where fortified cities and descendants of Anak remain. His confidence is neither denial of difficulty nor confidence in youthful strength: “Perhaps the LORD will be with me and I will drive them out as the LORD promised.”

Joshua blesses him, and Hebron becomes Caleb's inheritance.

Chapter 15 details Judah's territory. Long boundary descriptions can feel remote, but they show promise becoming geography. God's pledge to Abraham is being mapped into actual towns, valleys, and borders.

Caleb drives the Anakim from Hebron. His nephew Othniel captures Kiriath-sepher and marries Caleb's daughter Achsah.

Achsah then asks her father for springs because her allotted land is in the Negev. Caleb gives her both upper and lower springs. Her initiative resembles Zelophehad's daughters: women within Israel's inheritance system actively seek provision rather than functioning merely as background figures.

The chapter ends with an important qualification: Judah cannot drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem, so they continue there.

That single verse again prevents us from imagining the conquest as complete extermination.

Theologically, these chapters live between “already” and “not yet.” God has truly given the land, decisive victories have occurred, and inheritance is being distributed—yet enemies remain and possession is incomplete.

That pattern becomes important throughout Scripture. God's promise can be certain before its fulfillment is fully visible.
difficult:
The extensive geographical boundaries are difficult to reconstruct because many ancient sites are uncertain. Their theological function does not depend on identifying every modern location.

Caleb's “completely” following God describes covenant faithfulness in the spy crisis, not moral perfection.

The persistence of Jebusites and other Canaanites is important when interpreting earlier “all” and “none left” conquest language. Joshua itself presents both decisive victory and incomplete occupation.
connections:
Hebrews later uses inheritance and rest language to show that Canaan was real fulfillment but not final fulfillment. A greater rest still remained.

Caleb's faith is confidence in God's promise in the face of genuine obstacles, not confidence in his own power.

The “already/not yet” shape has a Christian parallel: Christ's victory is accomplished, yet believers still await resurrection and the full renewal of creation.

title: Joseph's Inheritance, Zelophehad's Daughters, and Iron Chariots
explanation:
Chapters 16–17 assign territory to the descendants of Joseph—Ephraim and Manasseh. These chapters contain geography that can be difficult to visualize, but beneath the boundary descriptions several important themes emerge.

Ephraim's allotment occupies an important central region of Canaan. Yet the chapter closes with a troubling sentence: “They did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer.” Instead, the Canaanites remain and are subjected to forced labor.

At first glance that may look like a successful compromise. Israel controls the population and gains workers. But it is not what God commanded.

This becomes a recurring pattern as Joshua moves toward Judges. Israel increasingly chooses coexistence and economic advantage where God had commanded the removal of idolatrous Canaanite influence. The compromise appears practical before its spiritual cost becomes visible.

Chapter 17 turns to Manasseh and again mentions the daughters of Zelophehad—Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.

Their father had died without sons. In Numbers they appealed to Moses for an inheritance, and God said their claim was right. Now Moses is dead, decades have passed, and they approach Eleazar and Joshua: “The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our male relatives.”

They receive it.

This is a small but important example of God's Word surviving a leadership transition. A promise does not expire because the person who first heard it is gone.

Then the tribes descended from Joseph complain to Joshua. They are numerous, they say, and one allotment is not enough.

Joshua tells them to clear the forested hill country and expand there. They answer that the hill country is insufficient and the Canaanites in the valleys have iron chariots.

Iron chariots were formidable. The phrase probably refers to chariots reinforced or fitted with iron rather than vehicles made entirely from solid iron. On open ground they gave Canaanite forces a serious tactical advantage.

Joshua does not deny the difficulty. He tells Joseph's descendants that because they are numerous and strong, they can clear the hill country and drive out the Canaanites despite their chariots.

The issue is not whether the chariots are genuinely dangerous. They are. The question is whether visible military superiority cancels God's promise.

That question reaches back to the spies in Numbers. Israel's first generation saw fortified cities and powerful enemies and concluded, “We can't.” Caleb and Joshua did not deny the facts; they interpreted the facts under God's promise.

Now another generation faces the same temptation.

These chapters therefore contain two different forms of reluctance. Ephraim tolerates Canaanites when domination is economically useful. Joseph's tribes hesitate when Canaanite technology looks intimidating.

One says, in effect, “We don't need to remove them.” The other says, “We can't remove them.”

Both risk allowing circumstances to overrule God's Word.

Yet the chapters are not mainly a motivational speech about overcoming personal obstacles. They concern Israel's particular land promise. Christians should not turn “iron chariots” into a guarantee that God will make every difficult project succeed.

The enduring truth is more grounded: God's Word remains trustworthy even when obedience is costly, inconvenient, or frightening.
difficult:
Forced labor does not represent complete obedience to the conquest command. Judges will make the consequences of Israel's compromises increasingly clear.

“Iron chariots” should not be mocked as though Israel's fear were irrational. They were advanced and dangerous military equipment. Faith is not pretending threats are imaginary.

The inheritance given to Zelophehad's daughters occurs within Israel's ancient tribal land system. Its significance includes God's concern that the promise He gave through Moses actually be honored.
connections:
The daughters' inheritance illustrates the continuity of God's promise: human leaders die, but God's Word remains.

The New Testament similarly distinguishes faith from sight. Faith does not deny visible difficulty; it trusts the God who has spoken.

At the same time, Christian faith does not turn Israel's specific conquest promises into promises of personal success. Our clearest promise is deeper: nothing can separate those in Christ from God's love, even when earthly circumstances remain difficult.

title: Shiloh, the Remaining Inheritance, and Cities of Refuge
explanation:
Chapter 18 opens with the whole Israelite community assembling at Shiloh and setting up the tent of meeting.

That is a major moment. The tabernacle that traveled through the wilderness now stands within the promised land. Shiloh will remain Israel's principal sanctuary for generations, into the time of Samuel.

Yet the very next sentence says seven tribes still have not received their inheritance.

Joshua asks them, “How long will you delay going out to take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your ancestors, gave you?”

The wording holds together gift and action. God has given the land, but the tribes are not therefore passive. They must receive, survey, settle, and possess what has been given.

Joshua sends twenty-one men—three from each remaining tribe—to survey the land and describe it in seven portions. The divisions are then assigned by lot “before the LORD” at Shiloh.

Casting lots here is not gambling for entertainment. Within Israel's covenant life it is a recognized means of distributing what God has already promised. Proverbs later says the lot is cast into the lap but its decision is from the LORD.

That does not mean Christians should roll dice whenever they want to know God's will. We have no general promise that random outcomes reveal God's hidden decisions. The normal Christian calling is to listen to God's revealed Word and exercise wisdom.

Benjamin receives the first allotment, lying between Judah and the Joseph tribes. Chapter 19 will continue the remaining allotments, but chapter 20 interrupts the territorial material to establish cities of refuge.

These cities were commanded in Numbers and Deuteronomy. A person who kills someone unintentionally can flee there from the “avenger of blood,” normally a close relative responsible for responding to the death.

The fugitive presents the case to the elders and receives protection until judicial proceedings can determine what happened.

The law recognizes a distinction that is morally fundamental: causing a death accidentally is not the same as murder.

At the same time, accidental killing is not treated casually. Bloodshed disrupts community life, and the killer cannot simply say, “I didn't mean it,” and continue as though nothing happened. There is investigation, refuge, and a structured process.

Six cities are designated—Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan—distributed on both sides of the Jordan.

The refuge is available not only to native Israelites but also to resident aliens and temporary residents. Justice is not supposed to depend on ethnicity.

There is an interesting movement across these chapters. Israel receives land as inheritance, but immediately that land must become a place where justice is practiced.

Possessing the promised land is not simply about having property. Israel is to become a community shaped by God's presence at Shiloh and God's concern for truthful judgment.

The tabernacle and the refuge city belong in the same world. The God who dwells among Israel is holy, and His holiness includes protection against vengeance outrunning justice.
difficult:
Joshua's question “How long will you delay?” concerns tribes who have a specific divine promise regarding Canaan. It should not be turned into a generic claim that every unfulfilled dream is something God has already given us.

Casting lots was used at particular points in biblical history, but Scripture does not command Christians to use randomness as a routine method of discovering God's will.

A city of refuge did not automatically acquit a killer. It protected the accused from immediate blood vengeance so the case could be heard.
connections:
The refuge-city system contributes to the Bible's distinction between justice and revenge. Personal vengeance is restrained by a community process.

Christian interpreters have sometimes used the cities as pictures of refuge in Christ. That can be a useful analogy if it is not mistaken for the chapter's original meaning.

Most importantly, Shiloh continues the great biblical theme of God dwelling among His people—a theme that reaches the temple and ultimately Christ, the Word who “dwelt” or “tabernacled” among us.

title: Not One Promise Failed—and a Crisis at the Jordan
explanation:
Chapter 21 assigns towns to the Levites. Unlike the other tribes, Levi does not receive one large territorial block. Forty-eight towns, with surrounding pasturelands, are distributed among the tribal territories.

This scattering fits Levi's calling. Priests and Levites are connected with worship, teaching, and service throughout Israel rather than forming a separate territorial kingdom.

The chapter then pauses for one of the strongest summaries in Joshua:

“The LORD gave Israel all the land he had sworn to give their ancestors.”

“The LORD gave them rest on every side.”

“None of the good promises the LORD had made to the house of Israel failed. Everything was fulfilled.”

That language must be held together with passages saying territory remains unconquered and Canaanites still live in parts of the land.

Joshua itself sees no contradiction. The promise has reached decisive historical fulfillment: Israel is established in Canaan, major resistance has been broken, tribal inheritances have been assigned, and the nation has rest from the great wars. Yet local possession remains incomplete.

This is an important biblical category: fulfillment can be genuine without yet being final or exhaustive.

Chapter 22 then threatens to shatter Israel's new rest almost immediately.

The warriors of Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh have completed the duty they accepted under Moses. Though their families live east of the Jordan, they crossed with Israel and fought until the western tribes received their inheritance.

Joshua commends their faithfulness, blesses them, and sends them home with substantial spoil.

Near the Jordan they build an enormous altar.

When the western tribes hear about it, they assume the eastern tribes have established a rival place of sacrifice. That would be serious apostasy. Israel has only recently heard God's command concerning worship at His chosen sanctuary.

The western tribes gather for war.

Their concern is not entirely unreasonable. They remember Peor, where idolatry brought plague, and Achan, whose individual sin brought judgment on Israel. They know rebellion can affect the whole covenant community.

But before attacking they send Phinehas and ten tribal leaders to investigate.

That step saves Israel from civil war.

The eastern tribes respond with an emphatic oath: “The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows.”

They explain that the altar is not for burnt offerings or sacrifices. It is a witness.

Their fear is that future western Israelites might look at the Jordan and tell the eastern tribes, “You have no share in the LORD.” The altar is meant to testify that both sides belong to the same covenant people who worship at the LORD's true altar.

Phinehas and the delegation are satisfied. The altar is named as a witness “that the LORD is God.”

The episode is remarkably relevant to communal conflict. The western tribes take doctrinal error seriously; they do not shrug and say worship does not matter. But they also do not make war solely on rumor. They investigate and allow the accused to explain.

Both instincts matter.

Joshua 21 says not one of God's good promises failed. Joshua 22 shows how quickly God's people can nearly destroy their own peace through misunderstanding.

God's faithfulness is perfect. The community receiving His gifts still needs patience, truth, and careful listening.
difficult:
“Everything was fulfilled” in Joshua 21 does not require that every Canaanite had disappeared. The book's own descriptions of remaining territory define the sense in which fulfillment is being claimed.

The altar in Joshua 22 was not a second sacrificial altar. The eastern tribes explicitly deny that purpose.

The western tribes' willingness to investigate before attacking should not be overlooked. Their initial conclusion is wrong, but they create a process in which the truth can emerge.
connections:
Hebrews 4 uses Joshua's “rest” to make a crucial point: if Joshua had given the final rest God intends, Scripture would not later speak of another day. Canaan was real fulfillment pointing beyond itself.

For Christians, Joshua 22 offers a valuable pattern for doctrinal disputes: truth matters, but accusation must not substitute for hearing.

The great declaration of Joshua 21 remains central: God's good Word did not fail. The Christian gospel rests on the same divine faithfulness, now centered in God's promises fulfilled in Christ.

title: Joshua's Farewell: The God Who Chose, Saved, and Kept His Word
explanation:
Joshua is now old, and the book closes with two farewell scenes.

In chapter 23 he gathers Israel's leaders and reminds them what they have seen: “You have seen for yourselves everything the LORD your God did to all these nations on your account, because it was the LORD your God who was fighting for you.”

Israel's future therefore depends neither on Joshua remaining alive nor on military momentum. The God who acted is still Israel's God.

Joshua urges them to hold firmly to Moses' instruction and avoid the idolatry of the nations remaining among them. He especially warns against covenant intermarriage that would draw Israel into worship of other gods.

The danger is spiritual assimilation. The remaining nations can become “a snare and a trap” if Israel abandons the LORD.

Joshua then says he is “going the way of all the earth”—he is about to die. Before he does, he reminds them that not one of God's promises has failed.

But the warning has another side. The God who faithfully fulfilled His good promises will also faithfully carry out covenant judgment if Israel abandons Him. Divine faithfulness is not mere niceness. God is faithful to His holiness as well as His mercy.

Chapter 24 gathers Israel at Shechem and retells the whole story.

The story begins before Abraham's call: Abraham's ancestors lived beyond the Euphrates and “worshiped other gods.”

That is significant. Israel's history does not begin with an exceptionally religious family searching until it found the true God.

God says, “I took your father Abraham.”

Then the divine verbs pile up: I gave, I sent, I afflicted Egypt, I brought you out, I brought you to the land, I handed your enemies over.

Israel's identity is founded on what God has done.

Only after this long recital of grace does Joshua say, “Therefore, fear the LORD and worship him in sincerity and truth.”

Then comes the famous line: “Choose for yourselves today: Which will you worship?”

Taken by itself, that verse can sound like a general formula for conversion based on autonomous human choice. In context, Joshua is addressing the covenant nation God has already chosen, redeemed, carried, and established. He is demanding that Israel abandon the idols it still clings to and live faithfully as the LORD's people.

“As for me and my family, we will worship the LORD.”

The people enthusiastically agree. Joshua's response is startling: “You will not be able to worship the LORD, because he is a holy God. He is a jealous God.”

Joshua is not encouraging idolatry. He is exposing glib self-confidence. Israel should not imagine covenant faithfulness is secured merely because everyone has made a strong public declaration.

The people insist, and Joshua renews the covenant, sets up a stone witness, and dismisses them to their inheritances.

Then Joshua dies at 110.

Joseph's bones, carried from Egypt according to his ancient request, are finally buried at Shechem. Eleazar the priest also dies.

The closing notices reach all the way back to Genesis. Joseph died believing God would bring Israel to this land. Centuries later, his bones are laid to rest there.

Joshua therefore ends with extraordinary fulfillment—and an unresolved question.

God has been faithful. Will Israel be?

The book of Judges will answer almost immediately.
difficult:
“Choose whom you will serve” must not be detached from the chapter's account of God's prior gracious action or Joshua's warning that Israel cannot casually promise faithfulness. It is not a proof-text for decision theology.

God's “jealousy” is covenant language, not insecure human envy. It describes His rightful refusal to share His people's worship with idols.

Joshua 23's warnings about intermarriage concern religious apostasy, not racial purity. Rahab and other outsiders can be incorporated into Israel when they identify with Israel's God.
connections:
The grace-before-command pattern is especially clear here: “I took... I gave... I brought...” comes before “therefore, serve.”

That fits the wider biblical gospel pattern and Lutheran theology. God does not wait for sinners to create saving faith by force of will; His Word calls, promises, and gives what faith receives.

Joseph's burial is also a quiet testimony to resurrection-shaped hope. Hebrews 11 remembers Joseph's instructions about his bones as an act of faith in God's future promise. Death did not make God's promise irrelevant.

title: The Cycle Begins: Israel Forgets the LORD
explanation:
Judges begins after Joshua's death, but its opening chapters deliberately contrast with Joshua's confident ending. Israel asks the LORD who should go first against the remaining Canaanites, and Judah is chosen. Early victories suggest continuity: God is still faithful and the conquest can continue.

Yet cracks quickly appear. Judah cannot drive out the inhabitants of the plain “because they had iron chariots.” Benjamin does not remove the Jebusites from Jerusalem. Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali likewise leave Canaanites in place, often putting them to forced labor instead.

The issue is not that Canaanite technology has somehow become stronger than God. Joshua had already confronted iron chariots. The repeated pattern is incomplete obedience. Israel increasingly settles for control, coexistence, or economic usefulness rather than carrying out the commission it had received.

Chapter 1 includes the brutal episode of Adoni-bezek, whose thumbs and big toes are cut off. He himself interprets it as retribution because he had mutilated seventy kings in the same way. The narrator records his recognition without turning mutilation into a general principle of biblical justice.

Caleb's family appears again. Othniel captures Kiriath-sepher, and Achsah asks her father Caleb for springs to make her land productive. Amid the growing failures, this family still resembles the faithful inheritance-taking seen in Joshua.

Chapter 2 supplies the theological key to the entire book. The angel of the LORD announces that God kept His covenant but Israel has not obeyed His voice. Israel weeps at Bochim and sacrifices, yet the narrative soon shows that tears alone do not create lasting faithfulness.

A generation arises “who did not know the LORD or the works he had done for Israel.” This does not necessarily mean they possessed no information about God. In biblical language, knowing the LORD involves covenant recognition and trust. The saving story has ceased to govern their lives.

Then comes the cycle that structures Judges: Israel abandons the LORD for the Baals and Ashtoreths; God's anger gives them into the hands of oppressors; Israel groans; God raises judges who save them; after the judge dies, they become corrupt again—often worse than before.

The judges are not primarily courtroom officials. They are deliverers whom God raises to rescue Israel from oppression.

Verse 18 is especially important: God is moved by Israel's groaning under those who afflict them. His deliverance repeatedly springs from compassion even though Israel's repentance is inconsistent.

But the spiral is downward. The book is not a collection of uncomplicated heroes showing us how to become brave. Many judges themselves become increasingly compromised.

God leaves some nations in the land to test Israel. This does not mean He causes Israel's idolatry. Their choices reveal whether they will listen to His commands.

Judges therefore begins with a sobering truth: receiving God's gifts does not eliminate the human heart's tendency to wander. Israel has the land, the law, the memory of mighty acts—and still needs a deeper rescue.
difficult:
The conquest material remains tied to Israel's unique covenant commission and must not be used to authorize Christian violence.

Judges 1 sometimes says a tribe “could not” drive people out, while chapter 2 interprets Israel's larger failure morally. Military difficulty was real, but it does not overturn the narrator's theological judgment.

The angel of the LORD is closely identified with God in several Judges narratives. Christian interpreters have sometimes identified these appearances with the pre-incarnate Christ, but the Old Testament itself does not explicitly settle that later Trinitarian identification.
connections:
Judges' cycle shows why external rescue alone cannot cure sin. Israel repeatedly receives deliverance and repeatedly returns to idolatry.

That prepares for the biblical promise of a new heart and ultimately for Christ's deeper deliverance from sin, death, and the devil.

It also warns against treating the Christian faith as inherited cultural memory. God's saving works must continually be proclaimed to the next generation through His Word.

title: Unexpected Deliverers: Ehud, Deborah, Barak, and Jael
explanation:
Judges 3 introduces the first named deliverers and establishes how surprising God's instruments can be.

Othniel is the most conventional judge. Israel serves the Baals, God gives them to Cushan-rishathaim, they cry out, and “the Spirit of the LORD came on him.” Othniel defeats the oppressor, and the land has forty years of rest.

Then the story becomes stranger.

Eglon king of Moab oppresses Israel for eighteen years. God raises Ehud, described as left-handed—literally perhaps restricted or bound in his right hand. In a culture expecting weapons on the usual side, his left-handedness helps him conceal a sword.

Ehud's assassination of the obese Eglon is narrated with dark, almost grotesque humor. The servants wait outside because they assume the king is relieving himself, giving Ehud time to escape. Israel then defeats Moab and enjoys eighty years of rest.

The story does not establish assassination as a Christian ethical model. It narrates deliverance in the violent political world of ancient Judges and emphasizes that God can use an unexpected person and method.

Shamgar receives only one verse: he kills six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad and also saves Israel. Even the brief notice reinforces that deliverance does not depend on conventional weapons.

Chapters 4–5 tell the same great victory twice—first in prose, then in poetry.

Deborah is both prophetess and judge. Israelites come to her for judgment, and she summons Barak with God's command to confront Sisera, commander of Jabin's army.

Barak says he will go only if Deborah goes with him. Interpreters disagree whether this is cowardice, prudent desire for the prophet's presence, or some mixture. Deborah agrees but says the honor of killing Sisera will go to a woman.

Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots, terrifying weapons on level terrain. Yet God routs his army. The song in chapter 5 suggests a storm and flooding of the Kishon River helped turn the battlefield against the chariots.

Sisera flees to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. She gives him milk, covers him, and when he sleeps drives a tent peg through his head.

Again, this is a disturbing war story. Judges celebrates Jael's act as the defeat of an oppressor, but Christians are not thereby given permission to imitate wartime killing in ordinary relationships.

The Song of Deborah interprets the victory as God's action: “LORD, when you came from Seir... the earth trembled.” It also criticizes tribes that stayed home while others risked themselves.

The poem ends, “LORD, may all your enemies perish as Sisera did. But may those who love him be like the rising of the sun in its strength.”

Then the land has rest for forty years.

These chapters are not polished moral biographies. Ehud deceives and kills; Jael violates expectations of hospitality; Barak's motives are debated. Yet God hears oppressed Israel and acts through people no Canaanite military planner would have chosen.

Judges continually shifts attention from impressive human qualifications to the God who raises deliverers.
difficult:
Deborah's leadership is presented positively; the text never says her role is God's punishment for lack of qualified men. Barak is also commended in Hebrews 11.

Jael's killing of Sisera occurs in a wartime context and is praised in the victory song. That does not make deceptive killing a universal moral norm.

The Song of Deborah is poetry and may describe the battle with vivid cosmic imagery. Its storm language plausibly explains how chariot superiority was neutralized, but the exact meteorological sequence is not given.
connections:
Hebrews 11 names Barak among examples of faith, reminding us not to reduce him to a caricature of cowardice.

The pattern remains grace first: Israel has again done evil, yet God hears and raises a savior.

These temporary saviors point beyond themselves. They defeat particular oppressors for a time; Christ's victory addresses the deeper enemies no judge can permanently defeat.

title: Gideon: Weakness, Signs, and an Army Made Smaller
explanation:
Israel again does evil, and Midian devastates the land for seven years. The Midianites arrive at harvest like locusts, destroying crops and livestock. Israelites hide in caves and strongholds.

When they cry to God, He first sends a prophet. Before rescue comes interpretation: Israel's misery is connected to abandoning the God who brought them from Egypt.

Then the angel of the LORD appears to Gideon while he is threshing wheat in a winepress—an awkward hidden location chosen because he fears Midian.

The greeting sounds almost ironic: “The LORD is with you, valiant warrior.”

Gideon's first response is not confidence but complaint: if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened? Where are the wonders our ancestors told us about?

God does not shame him for asking. He commissions him: “Go in the strength you have and deliver Israel.”

Gideon immediately protests that his clan is weakest and he is least in his family. God's answer is the real foundation: “But I will be with you.”

Gideon asks for a sign, and fire consumes his offering. He realizes with terror that he has encountered the angel of the LORD, but God tells him, “Peace to you. Don't be afraid.”

His first assignment is not against Midian but against his father's Baal altar. Gideon destroys it at night because he is afraid. His action is obedient even though his courage is incomplete.

The townsmen want him killed, but his father Joash replies that if Baal is really a god, Baal can defend himself. Gideon receives the name Jerubbaal—“Let Baal contend.”

The Spirit of the LORD then “clothed” Gideon, and tribes gather to him.

Gideon's fleece follows. He asks for dew on the fleece but dry ground, then the reverse.

This is often taught as a method for discovering God's will: “put out a fleece.” But Gideon already knows God's will. God has explicitly commissioned him. The fleece is reassurance for a fearful man, not a model for manufacturing signs when Scripture has given us no promise of one.

God graciously accommodates Gideon's weakness.

Chapter 7 then makes Gideon's army absurdly small. From 32,000 men, the fearful are dismissed, leaving 10,000. A water-drinking test reduces them to 300.

God states the reason: with a large army, Israel might boast, “My own strength saved me.”

Before the attack, God gives Gideon another reassurance. He overhears a Midianite interpreting a dream as Gideon's victory. Gideon worships.

The 300 men surround the camp with trumpets, jars, and torches. At the signal they smash the jars, reveal the lights, blow trumpets, and shout. God throws Midian into panic, and the enemy turns swords against itself.

The point is not that 300 spiritually elite men can accomplish anything if sufficiently brave. The army is deliberately inadequate so that Israel cannot plausibly claim the victory.

Gideon's weakness is not an obstacle God reluctantly overcomes. It becomes the setting in which God's saving power is unmistakable.
difficult:
The fleece episode is descriptive, not a promised Christian technique for discerning God's will. Repeatedly demanding arbitrary signs can become a way of avoiding ordinary wisdom and God's revealed Word.

The reduction to 300 is explicitly designed to prevent boasting. The text does not say the 300 were chosen because their drinking posture proved superior vigilance; that popular explanation is not in Judges.

The angel of the LORD speaks with divine authority, but the precise relationship between angelic manifestation and the LORD remains mysterious in the Old Testament.
connections:
Paul's language in 1 Corinthians about God choosing what is weak so no one may boast resonates strongly with Gideon's story.

God's word to Gideon—“I will be with you”—is more important than Gideon's self-assessment.

The cross gives this pattern its fullest expression: God's saving power appears in what the world calls weakness, leaving no room for sinners to boast in themselves.

title: Gideon's Success Becomes a Snare
explanation:
Chapter 8 deliberately complicates the Gideon story. The frightened man of chapter 6 has become a victorious commander, but success begins exposing new dangers.

The Ephraimites angrily confront Gideon for not summoning them earlier. Gideon answers diplomatically, praising their contribution, and their anger subsides. At first he handles conflict wisely.

But when Gideon pursues the remaining Midianite kings, the towns of Succoth and Penuel refuse to feed his exhausted troops. After victory he returns and punishes them harshly—beating Succoth's elders with thorns and tearing down Penuel's tower, killing men there.

The narrative does not explicitly commend this vengeance. Gideon's behavior is becoming more severe and personally driven.

He then learns that the Midianite kings killed his brothers. His execution of them therefore carries a personal blood-feud dimension as well as military judgment.

Israel offers Gideon hereditary kingship: “Rule over us, you as well as your sons and your grandsons, for you delivered us from the power of Midian.”
