Gideon gives the correct theological answer: “I will not rule over you... the LORD will rule over you.”

But his actions immediately look remarkably royal.

He asks for gold from the spoil and makes an ephod weighing about seventeen hundred shekels of gold. Israel prostitutes itself by worshiping it, and it becomes “a snare to Gideon and his household.”

Gideon also has many wives and seventy sons. His concubine in Shechem bears a son whom he names Abimelech—“my father is king.”

So Gideon verbally rejects kingship while living increasingly like a king.

This is one of Judges' central lessons: a deliverer can become part of the problem.

Chapter 9 shows the fruit. Abimelech persuades his mother's relatives in Shechem to support him, hires reckless men, and murders his seventy brothers on one stone. Only Jotham escapes.

Jotham tells the famous fable of the trees seeking a king. The productive olive, fig, and vine refuse to abandon their useful work, but the worthless bramble eagerly offers to rule—and threatens fire.

Abimelech is the bramble king.

God sends division between Abimelech and Shechem. Violence consumes the alliance that violence created. Abimelech destroys Shechem but eventually dies when a woman drops an upper millstone on his head. To avoid the shame of being said to have been killed by a woman, he orders his armor-bearer to finish him.

The narrator interprets the outcome plainly: God repaid Abimelech for murdering his brothers and repaid Shechem for supporting him.

Chapter 10 briefly mentions Tola and Jair, then returns to Israel's worsening apostasy. The list of foreign gods grows longer.

When Israel cries out, God initially answers with biting irony: go cry to the gods you chose.

Israel finally removes the foreign gods and serves the LORD, and then comes one of the most moving lines in Judges: God “became weary of Israel's misery,” or, more literally, His soul could no longer bear their suffering.

Israel's repentance is imperfect, but God's compassion remains astonishing.

The cycle continues—not because Israel has found a better hero, but because the LORD continues to have mercy on people who repeatedly ruin His gifts.
difficult:
Gideon's ephod may have been intended as a religious memorial or priestly object, but it becomes an idol. Good intentions do not make unauthorized worship safe.

Judges does not simply divide characters into heroes and villains. Gideon is genuinely used by God and later behaves in troubling ways.

God's statement in chapter 10 that He will no longer save Israel is followed by renewed compassion. This is not divine fickleness; the dialogue exposes Israel's false worship and moves toward the mercy that repeatedly characterizes God.
connections:
Gideon's refusal of kingship followed by king-like behavior prepares for Judges' larger question about righteous rule.

Human deliverers repeatedly fail under the weight of their own sin. The Bible's hope increasingly requires a king who will not use power for himself.

God's compassion toward miserable Israel also reminds us that salvation rests finally in His mercy, not the consistency of His people's repentance.

title: Jephthah's Vow: A Deliverer Trapped by His Own Words
explanation:
Jephthah is introduced as a “valiant warrior” and the son of a prostitute. His half-brothers drive him away so he will receive no inheritance. He gathers a band of adventurers around him in Tob.

When the Ammonites threaten Gilead, the elders who rejected him now ask him to lead them. Jephthah makes them promise that if God gives him victory, he will become their head.

His negotiations with the Ammonite king show that Jephthah knows Israel's history. He argues that Israel did not seize Moabite or Ammonite territory during the Exodus; the disputed land was taken from Sihon the Amorite after Sihon attacked Israel.

Then “the Spirit of the LORD came on Jephthah.”

That statement means God empowers him for deliverance. It does not mean every subsequent decision Jephthah makes is inspired or approved.

Before battle Jephthah makes his notorious vow: if God gives him victory, “whatever comes out of the doors of my house to greet me when I return... will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it as a burnt offering.”

God has already empowered Jephthah. The vow is unnecessary.

Jephthah wins, and his only child—a daughter—comes out to meet him with tambourines and dancing.

The story is devastating.

Interpreters have long debated what happens next. The straightforward reading is that Jephthah sacrifices his daughter. Some argue that she is instead devoted to lifelong virginity, pointing to the repeated emphasis on her virginity and the wording that she “never knew a man.”

But “offer it as a burnt offering” normally means sacrifice, and the text says Jephthah “carried out his vow with her.” The tragic-sacrifice reading remains the more natural one.

Crucially, the text never says God commanded the vow or demanded its fulfillment. Human sacrifice is forbidden in Israel's law. Jephthah's action should not be defended merely because he is a judge.

Judges is showing Israel becoming increasingly shaped by the violent religious world around it.

The daughter is the most admirable person in the scene. She bears the consequences of her father's reckless words, and Israelite women commemorate her annually.

Chapter 12 then turns from external warfare to tribal civil conflict. Ephraim again complains about not being summoned, as it did with Gideon. This time diplomacy fails.

Jephthah's Gileadites fight Ephraim and control the Jordan crossings. They identify fleeing Ephraimites by asking them to pronounce *Shibboleth*. Ephraimite pronunciation gives them away, and forty-two thousand die.

A word becomes a life-or-death identity test.

The chapter closes with three minor judges, but the damage is clear. Israel's deliverer has made a disastrous vow, and Israelites are slaughtering Israelites.

The downward spiral of Judges is accelerating.

Jephthah is listed in Hebrews 11 among people associated with faith, so we should not reduce his entire life to this sin. But neither should that commendation force us to call his vow righteous.

God can truly use deeply flawed people without endorsing everything they do.
difficult:
Jephthah's daughter is one of Scripture's hardest narratives. The sacrificial reading best fits “burnt offering,” though the lifelong-dedication view has a long history. Either way, the vow is rash and tragic, not a model of faithfulness.

The Spirit coming on Jephthah occurs before the vow. He did not need to bargain with God to secure victory.

Biblical vows never authorize what God has forbidden. A sinful promise does not become righteous merely because it was spoken solemnly.
connections:
Hebrews 11 names Jephthah without endorsing every action of his life, just as Scripture can recognize faith in deeply imperfect people.

The tragedy exposes the need for a deliverer whose own sin does not endanger those he saves.

Christ is the opposite of Jephthah at the decisive point: He does not sacrifice another person because of His rashness; He willingly gives Himself for others.

title: Samson: Set Apart from Birth, Yet Ruled by His Desires
explanation:
The Samson cycle begins differently from the earlier judges. Israel again does evil and is handed to the Philistines for forty years, but this time the text records no cry for help.

God begins the rescue anyway.

A childless woman, Manoah's wife, receives an announcement from the angel of the LORD: she will conceive and bear a son. The child is to be a Nazirite from the womb, and “he will begin to save Israel from the power of the Philistines.”

“Begin” matters. Samson will never complete the deliverance.

The Nazirite calling normally involved abstaining from grape products, avoiding corpse contamination, and not cutting the hair. Samson's life will repeatedly strain or violate the spirit of this consecration.

Manoah asks the angel to return and explain how to raise the child. When Manoah offers food, the angel directs sacrifice to the LORD. As the flame rises from the altar, the angel ascends in it.

Manoah fears they will die because they have seen God. His wife reasons more clearly: if God intended to kill them, He would not have accepted their offering or promised them a child.

Samson grows, God blesses him, and the Spirit begins to stir him.

Chapter 14 immediately reveals the problem. Samson sees a Philistine woman and tells his parents, essentially, “Get her for me, because she is right in my eyes.”

That phrase anticipates the book's refrain: everyone doing what is right in his own eyes.

His parents object, but the narrator adds that they do not know “this was from the LORD, who wanted the Philistines to provide an opportunity for a confrontation.”

This does not mean Samson's lust or disregard for covenant boundaries is morally approved. God sovereignly uses even Samson's disordered desires within His purpose against Philistia.

On the journey Samson tears apart a lion when the Spirit rushes upon him. Later he takes honey from the lion's carcass, creating tension with Nazirite corpse purity.

At his wedding feast he poses a riddle based on the lion and honey. The Philistines threaten his bride, she pressures Samson, and the riddle becomes an occasion for violence. Samson kills thirty Philistines at Ashkelon to pay the wager.

Chapter 15 escalates the feud. Samson's wife has been given to another man. Samson burns Philistine crops using foxes or jackals with torches. The Philistines retaliate by burning the woman and her father. Samson retaliates again.

This is not clean heroic warfare. It is a cycle of personal vengeance through which God nevertheless begins weakening Philistine domination.

Judah's men even hand Samson over to the Philistines because they fear their rulers. The tribe has become so accustomed to oppression that it treats its own God-given deliverer as the problem.

The Spirit rushes on Samson, his ropes fall away, and he kills a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone.

Then the mighty warrior nearly dies of thirst and cries to God. God provides water.

Samson's story continually juxtaposes extraordinary divine gift with extraordinary personal disorder. His strength is from God; his impulses are often his own.

The presence of God's gifts must never be confused with maturity of character.
difficult:
God's use of Samson's Philistine marriage as an “occasion” does not mean God approves Samson's motives. Divine providence can work through sinful human choices without making the sin good.

Samson's Nazirite status is unusual because it begins before birth by divine command. His contact with carcasses and later haircut highlight the unraveling of that consecration.

The Hebrew term for the animals used to burn the fields can refer to foxes or jackals. The exact species does not affect the point of the episode.
connections:
Samson's miraculous birth belongs to a biblical pattern in which God brings life where human strength cannot produce it.

Yet Samson is no ideal savior. His calling and character increasingly diverge.

That contrast prepares us to appreciate Christ: truly consecrated from birth, empowered by the Spirit, yet unlike Samson perfectly obedient rather than ruled by appetite and vengeance.

title: Samson Falls—and Israel Makes God in Its Own Image
explanation:
Chapter 16 brings Samson's contradictions to their climax.

He visits a prostitute in Gaza. The Philistines plan to kill him at dawn, but at midnight Samson tears the city gates from their posts and carries them away.

His God-given strength remains astonishing, but the narrative gives no indication that his sexual behavior is acceptable.

Then Samson loves Delilah in the Valley of Sorek. Philistine rulers each promise her silver if she discovers the source of his strength.

Three times Samson deceives her with false explanations. Three times she tests them. The danger could hardly be clearer.

Eventually Samson tells her “all his heart”: his hair has never been cut because he has been a Nazirite to God from birth.

It would be too simplistic to imagine Samson's hair as a magical battery. His strength comes from God. The uncut hair is the visible sign of a consecration Samson has progressively treated with contempt.

Delilah has his hair shaved while he sleeps. Samson wakes and says, “I will escape as I did before and shake myself free.”

Then comes the terrible sentence: “He did not know that the LORD had left him.”

Samson has begun to presume that divine power is simply his possession.

The Philistines blind him, bind him, and make him grind grain in prison.

“But his hair began to grow back.”

The line is quiet but hopeful. The point is not merely that his physical power is recharging. Samson's story is not quite over.

At a great feast to Dagon, the Philistines bring Samson out for entertainment. He asks God to remember him and strengthen him once more. He pushes down the supporting pillars, killing himself and thousands of Philistines.

The narrator says he kills more in his death than in his life.

Samson's final prayer includes personal vengeance for his eyes, so even at the end his motives are mixed. Yet Hebrews later remembers him among people of faith. God's grace does not require us to rewrite Samson into a morally spotless hero.

Chapter 17 abruptly shifts from national deliverers to private religious chaos.

A man named Micah steals silver from his mother, confesses, and returns it. She dedicates the silver to the LORD—and then uses part of it to make a carved idol.

That contradiction captures the age. People use the LORD's name while worshiping Him in ways He explicitly forbade.

Micah builds a shrine, makes an ephod and household gods, and installs one of his sons as priest even though priestly service belongs to the Levites.

Then a wandering Levite arrives. Micah hires him as a private priest and concludes, “Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest.”

Religion has become a technique for obtaining blessing.

The chapter's explanation is famous: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did whatever seemed right to him.”

The problem is not merely lack of centralized government. It is moral autonomy—people constructing worship according to what seems right to them while still attaching God's name to it.

Samson presumed on God's power. Micah presumes he can arrange God's favor.

Both chapters expose the same deeper disorder: God's gifts are being treated as possessions humans can manipulate.
difficult:
Samson's hair is a covenant sign of his Nazirite consecration, not magic. Judges explicitly attributes his extraordinary power to the Spirit of the LORD.

His suicide-like final act occurs in the context of Israel's warfare with Philistia and his calling as judge. It should not be used to justify suicide or self-destructive violence.

Micah's religious language does not make his shrine legitimate. The narrator expects readers who know the Torah to recognize the violations.
connections:
Hebrews 11's inclusion of Samson shows that faith can coexist with grievous weakness without making the weakness virtuous.

Samson saves through his death in a limited and violent sense, which can create a faint typological contrast with Christ. But the differences are greater: Jesus willingly dies in holy love for sinners rather than vengeance for Himself.

Micah's shrine warns against treating worship as a human method for controlling God's blessing. Grace is received on God's terms, not manufactured by religious technique.

title: Idolatry and Horror: Israel Becomes Like Canaan
explanation:
Judges 18 continues Micah's story and shows private idolatry becoming tribal.

The tribe of Dan has not secured its allotted inheritance, so five scouts search for another territory. They encounter Micah's Levite and ask him to seek God's guidance. The Levite assures them their journey has the LORD's approval.

But the entire religious arrangement is corrupt. A person speaking religious words from an unauthorized shrine is not made trustworthy by sounding confident.

The scouts find Laish, a peaceful and isolated town. Six hundred Danite warriors return to seize it.

On the way they steal Micah's carved image, ephod, household gods, and priest. When the Levite protests, they offer him a promotion: is it better to be priest for one household or an entire tribe?

He is pleased.

That sentence exposes him. Ministry has become career advancement.

Micah pursues them but realizes he cannot overcome the larger force. His cry is tragically ironic: “You took the gods I made and my priest and went away. What do I have left?”

A god that can be stolen is no god at all.

Dan destroys Laish and establishes the stolen idol there. The narrator identifies the priest as Jonathan, a descendant of Moses (some manuscripts obscure the name slightly, apparently because of the shame attached to it). The point is shocking: even a family connected to Moses can descend into idolatry.

Chapter 19 is darker still.

A Levite takes a concubine from Bethlehem. After a separation, he goes to retrieve her. On the return journey he refuses to stay in a foreign Jebusite city and instead chooses Gibeah, an Israelite town in Benjamin—presumably expecting greater safety among God's covenant people.

No one initially offers hospitality except an elderly man.

Then men of the city surround the house and demand to sexually assault the Levite. The scene deliberately echoes Sodom in Genesis 19.

But this is not Sodom. It is Israel.

The host offers his daughter and the Levite's concubine—an appalling act that the narrative does not endorse. Eventually the Levite pushes his concubine outside. The mob abuses her through the night, and she collapses at the doorway.

The Levite finds her in the morning and says, “Get up. Let's go.” There is no tenderness. When she does not respond, he places her on his donkey, takes her home, cuts her body into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout Israel.

The text does not explicitly tell us whether she was already dead when he found her; later language treats her as murdered. The ambiguity makes the Levite's conduct no less horrifying.

Judges has reached a point where the people who were supposed to be distinct from Canaan reproduce the wickedness associated with Canaan.

The repeated refrain “there was no king in Israel” frames this collapse. But merely having a human monarch will not solve the heart's problem; Israel's later kings can also become corrupt.

The reader is being made to long for righteous rule—for a king who will truly lead God's people in justice rather than everyone doing what is right in his own eyes.
difficult:
Judges 19 is descriptive, not prescriptive. The host's offer and the Levite's surrender of the woman are morally horrifying and should never be defended simply because biblical characters do them.

The crime includes attempted male rape and the gang rape of a woman. The central issue is violent sexual domination and radical violation of hospitality and human dignity; it should not be reduced to a simplistic slogan about one modern sexual category.

The textual form of Jonathan's ancestry in Judges 18 has a scribal peculiarity. The likely original reading connects him to Moses, which intensifies the story's scandal.
connections:
Judges 19 intentionally echoes Sodom to show that covenant privilege has not automatically made Israel righteous.

The Levite's failure to protect the vulnerable contrasts sharply with Christ, who gives Himself for His people rather than handing another over to save Himself.

The longing for a righteous king grows stronger—but the rest of Scripture will show that Israel needs more than political centralization. It needs a faithful king and renewed hearts.

title: Civil War and the Collapse of Israel
explanation:
The mutilated body sent throughout Israel produces national outrage. The tribes assemble “as one man” and demand an account of what happened at Gibeah.

The Levite tells the story, but his version is selective. He emphasizes Gibeah's intention to kill him and the abuse of his concubine while omitting that he himself handed her over.

That should caution us against assuming a narrator inside the story is giving a morally complete account merely because his words are recorded in Scripture.

Israel demands that Benjamin surrender the guilty men of Gibeah. Benjamin refuses and instead mobilizes for war.

A local atrocity now becomes tribal solidarity with evil.

Israel asks God who should go first, and Judah is named. Yet Benjamin defeats Israel on the first day and again on the second, killing tens of thousands.

This is unsettling. Israel has sought God's direction, but obedience does not produce immediate victory.

On the third day the Israelites weep, fast, offer sacrifices, and inquire again. Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, is serving before the ark—an important chronological clue that these terrible events may have occurred relatively early in the Judges period even though they are placed at the book's end to display Israel's moral collapse.

God promises victory, and Benjamin is devastated. Only six hundred men escape.

Then Israel realizes it has nearly eliminated one of the twelve tribes.

But its attempted solution reveals that the moral confusion has not ended.

The Israelites had sworn not to give their daughters to Benjamin. They also discover that no one from Jabesh-gilead came to the assembly, so they send troops to destroy that town, sparing four hundred virgin women to give to surviving Benjaminites.

Still short of wives, they tell the remaining Benjaminites to hide near Shiloh and abduct young women who come out to dance at a festival.

The book does not present this as clever obedience.

Israel has responded to the horrific abuse of one woman by creating circumstances in which hundreds of other women are killed, seized, or abducted.

Oaths made rashly are maneuvered around rather than the underlying moral disaster being confronted.

Judges ends with the refrain: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did whatever seemed right to him.”

The final chapters have made that sentence concrete. Religious corruption led to social corruption; social corruption led to sexual violence; outrage led to civil war; civil war led to near-genocide; and attempts to repair the damage produced further violence against women.

The downward spiral is complete.

Yet the phrase about no king creates an expectation that the next stage of Israel's story will involve monarchy. Samuel and Kings will explore that hope.

The answer will be complicated. A righteous king can restrain evil, but a sinful king can magnify it. Saul, David, Solomon, and their successors will prove that political structure alone cannot heal the human heart.

Judges leaves the reader wanting more than another judge and ultimately more than an ordinary king.

Israel needs a deliverer who does not become part of the problem.
difficult:
The final chapters are intentionally horrific. Their presence in Scripture does not signal approval; the narrator is showing what covenant collapse looks like.

Israel's first two defeats do not mean God approves Benjamin's defense of Gibeah. The eventual divine answer makes clear that Benjamin will be handed over.

The massacre at Jabesh-gilead and abduction at Shiloh should not be defended as morally exemplary solutions. They belong to the very chaos summarized by the book's closing verdict.
connections:
Judges creates a longing for righteous kingship, which the story of David will partially answer. But later history proves that even David's house needs redemption.

The Christian canonical answer is not simply “Israel needed stronger government.” It needed the true King.

Jesus does not rescue by exploiting the vulnerable or preserving Himself at their expense. He bears judgment Himself and establishes a kingdom characterized by righteousness, mercy, and peace. Judges' darkness helps us feel why that kind of King is necessary.

title: From Emptiness to the Field of Boaz
explanation:
Ruth opens “during the time of the judges.” After the moral darkness at the end of Judges, that setting matters. Ruth shows that God is still quietly preserving faithfulness in ordinary homes and fields.

A famine drives Elimelech, Naomi, and their two sons from Bethlehem—ironically, the “house of bread”—to Moab. Moab carries difficult biblical associations. Its origins are traced to Lot, it opposed Israel during the wilderness years, and Deuteronomy places restrictions on Moabite participation in Israel's assembly.

Then Naomi's life collapses. Elimelech dies. Her sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, but after about ten years both sons die as well. Naomi is left without husband or sons in a world where those losses also meant severe economic vulnerability.

Hearing that the LORD has again provided food in Judah, Naomi decides to return. She urges her daughters-in-law to remain in Moab, remarry, and build new lives.

Orpah eventually does what Naomi asks. The narrative does not portray her as wicked.

Ruth, however, clings to Naomi and speaks one of Scripture's great declarations of loyalty: where Naomi goes, Ruth will go; Naomi's people will be her people, and Naomi's God her God.

This is more than affection between two women. Ruth is leaving homeland, kinship, security, and the gods of Moab to identify herself with Naomi and Israel's God.

When they reach Bethlehem, Naomi says, “Don't call me Naomi. Call me Mara,” changing “pleasant” to “bitter.” She says she went away full and the LORD has brought her back empty.

Her lament is painfully honest. She attributes her suffering to God's hand because she believes God truly governs life. The narrator does not rebuke her for lamenting.

Yet Naomi's claim to be completely empty is already being quietly contradicted. Ruth is standing beside her.

The chapter ends with another small note of hope: they arrive at the beginning of barley harvest.

Chapter 2 introduces Boaz, a relative of Elimelech and a man of standing. Ruth asks permission to glean behind harvesters.

Israel's law required landowners not to reap every edge or pick up every fallen stalk. Those remnants were left for the poor and resident alien. This was not merely private charity; God's covenant law built provision for vulnerable people into Israel's economic life.

Then comes one of Ruth's characteristic providence statements: Ruth “happened to be” in the field belonging to Boaz.

From Ruth's perspective it is chance. From the narrator's perspective, the reader is invited to see God's quiet ordering of ordinary events.

Boaz has heard of Ruth's loyalty. He tells her to remain with his female workers, orders the men not to touch her, gives her water, and later instructs his workers deliberately to pull grain from bundles for her.

Ruth asks why she, a foreigner, has received such favor.

Boaz answers by describing what she has done for Naomi and says, “May the LORD reward you... under whose wings you have come for refuge.”

That image becomes important later. Ruth has sought refuge under God's wings, and God provides that refuge through the concrete faithfulness of Boaz.

At the end of the day Ruth brings Naomi an unusually large amount of barley. When Naomi learns whose field it is, her despair begins to lift: Boaz is one of their *go'el*—their family redeemers.

The word can describe a close relative responsible for protecting family interests, redeeming property, and in certain contexts avenging blood. Ruth will combine family-redemption themes with the need to preserve a dead man's family line.

God has not spoken audibly. No sea has divided. No angel has appeared.

But food has returned to Bethlehem, Ruth has entered one particular field, and a faithful relative has noticed her.

Ruth teaches us to recognize providence not only in miracles but in ordinary means through which God preserves and provides.
difficult:
Naomi's statement that God has made her life bitter should be heard as lament, not a complete theological explanation of why her husband and sons died. Ruth never tells us that these deaths were punishment for particular sins.

Ruth's Moabite identity is repeatedly emphasized. Whatever the precise application of Deuteronomy 23's restriction concerning Moabites, Ruth's inclusion makes clear that trust in Israel's God is not blocked by ethnic ancestry.

“Family redeemer” should not be reduced to “the man Ruth is supposed to marry.” The *go'el* institution involves broader kinship obligations, and Ruth 3–4 creatively brings together redemption, land, marriage, and preservation of the family line.
connections:
Boaz's blessing that Ruth has taken refuge under the LORD's wings becomes concrete through his own protection. God's providence often works through ordinary human vocations and acts of mercy.

Ruth's movement from foreigner to member of Israel anticipates the biblical promise that God's blessing through Abraham will reach the nations.

The story will ultimately place this Moabite widow in David's ancestry and, through David, in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Grace is already at work through people Israel might least expect.

title: At the Threshing Floor: Redemption, Rest, and the Line of David
explanation:
Naomi now seeks “rest” or security for Ruth. She identifies Boaz as a family redeemer and devises a bold plan involving the threshing floor.

After Boaz has eaten and lain down near the grain, Ruth approaches quietly, uncovers his feet, and lies down. Around midnight Boaz awakens and asks who she is.

Ruth replies, “I am Ruth, your servant. Take me under your wing, for you are a family redeemer.”

The wording deliberately echoes Boaz's earlier blessing that Ruth had sought refuge under the LORD's wings. Ruth is now asking Boaz to become, in a concrete way, an instrument of that divine shelter.

The threshing-floor scene is sexually suggestive enough to create tension, but the narrative goes out of its way to emphasize Ruth's and Boaz's honorable conduct. “Feet” can occasionally function as a euphemism elsewhere in Scripture, so some interpreters see more sexual implication in the scene. But Ruth does not say they had intercourse, and Boaz's later public actions make sense precisely because the marriage has not yet occurred.

Boaz praises Ruth's *hesed*—her covenant-like loyalty or steadfast kindness. She could have pursued younger men, but instead she is seeking a solution that preserves Naomi's family.

Boaz is willing, but there is a complication: another relative has a stronger claim to act as redeemer.

This is important for Boaz's character. He does not exploit the secrecy of the night to take what he wants. He submits the matter to the lawful process.

He sends Ruth home before daylight with a generous amount of barley. Naomi recognizes that Boaz will not rest until the matter is settled.

Chapter 4 moves to the city gate, where legal and commercial matters are conducted publicly. Boaz gathers the nearer redeemer and ten elders.

At first the nearer relative is willing to redeem Naomi's land. But when Boaz explains that the arrangement includes Ruth and preserving the dead man's name with his inheritance, the man declines because he fears damaging his own estate.

The exact legal combination in Ruth is unusual. It resembles the levirate-marriage principle of Deuteronomy 25, though Boaz is not Ruth's brother-in-law, and it also uses the family-redemption system of Leviticus 25. The story is applying Israel's kinship institutions to protect a vulnerable family and preserve its inheritance.

The transaction is confirmed with a sandal, an old legal custom the narrator feels the need to explain.

Boaz publicly takes Ruth as his wife. God enables her to conceive, and she bears a son.

Then the focus unexpectedly returns to Naomi.

The women bless God because He has not left Naomi without a redeemer. They say Ruth, who loves Naomi, is “better to you than seven sons.”

That is an extraordinary statement in an ancient culture where sons carried enormous social importance. The foreign daughter-in-law whom Naomi initially tried to send away has become the means through which her family is restored.

Naomi holds the child, and the women name him Obed.

Then the narrator reveals where the entire story has been going: Obed fathers Jesse, and Jesse fathers David.

The little story of two widows, a harvest field, and a family property problem is part of God's preservation of Israel's royal line.

The genealogy reaches back to Perez, the son of Judah and Tamar. Tamar, like Ruth, was a woman whose unconventional situation became part of preserving Judah's family line.

Ruth began with famine, bereavement, and Naomi saying, “I came back empty.”

It ends with harvest, marriage, a child in Naomi's arms, and the genealogy of David.

Yet Ruth never promises that every bereaved person will receive the same earthly restoration. Its deeper comfort is that God's providence can be active when His hand is almost invisible.

Naomi could not see where her story was going.

The reader can.
difficult:
Ruth's actions at the threshing floor are bold and potentially risky, but the text portrays Ruth and Boaz as people of honorable character. Claims that the passage explicitly describes a sexual encounter go beyond what it says.

The nearer redeemer's concern about his inheritance probably reflects the economic consequences of acquiring property that would eventually belong to an heir preserving Elimelech's family line. The legal details are not fully explained.

The child is called a “redeemer” for Naomi in the women's blessing even though Boaz has served as the legal family redeemer. The language broadens redemption to the restoration of Naomi's threatened family future.
connections:
Matthew 1 explicitly includes Ruth in Jesus' genealogy: Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.

Boaz can appropriately be seen as a limited picture of redemptive action—he uses his position and resources to protect and restore. But Christ is not simply a larger Boaz; He redeems from sin and death at the cost of His own life.

Ruth also provides a beautiful bridge from Judges to Samuel. Judges ends with Israel desperately needing righteous kingship. Ruth ends by quietly naming David's grandfather. Before Israel knows it needs David, God is already preserving the family through which David will come—and ultimately the Son of David.

title: Hannah's Prayer and the Great Reversal
explanation:
First Samuel begins not in a palace or battlefield but with a grieving woman in a divided household. Elkanah has two wives: Peninnah has children; Hannah does not. Peninnah repeatedly provokes Hannah because of her infertility.

The text never presents polygamy as an ideal. As elsewhere in the Old Testament, the family arrangement produces rivalry and pain.

Elkanah loves Hannah and gives her a special portion at the annual sacrifice at Shiloh, but his attempt to comfort her—“Am I not better to you than ten sons?”—does not remove her grief.

Hannah goes to the sanctuary and prays “with deep anguish.” She weeps bitterly and vows that if God gives her a son, she will give him to the LORD all his life and no razor will touch his head. The language resembles Nazirite dedication.

Eli the priest sees her lips moving without hearing her voice and assumes she is drunk. Hannah explains that she is pouring out her heart before the LORD.

Eli then blesses her, and the narrative says she leaves, eats, and is no longer downcast. The change comes before she knows whether she will conceive. She has entrusted her grief to God and received a word of blessing.

God “remembered” Hannah. As elsewhere in Scripture, remembering does not mean God had forgotten her and suddenly recalled her existence. It means He acts faithfully toward her.

She bears Samuel. His name is associated in the story with asking God for him, though the precise Hebrew wordplay is more complicated than a simple dictionary derivation.

Hannah keeps her vow. After Samuel is weaned, she brings him to Shiloh and gives him to the LORD's service.

Chapter 2 opens with Hannah's song. It is far more than a mother's private thank-you. It announces one of Samuel's great themes: God reverses human status.

The strong are broken; the weak are clothed with strength. The well-fed hire themselves out for bread; the hungry cease to hunger. The barren woman bears children. God brings low and raises up. He lifts the poor from the dust and seats them with nobles.

Then Hannah unexpectedly speaks of God's “king” and “anointed” even though Israel has not yet established a monarchy. The Hebrew word for “anointed” is *mashiach*—Messiah. In its immediate setting it anticipates Israel's coming king; within the whole biblical story, it opens a theme that will lead through David to Christ.

The chapter then contrasts Samuel with Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas.

They are priests but “did not know the LORD.” They seize the best portions of sacrifices before the fat has been offered to God and threaten worshipers who resist. They also sleep with women serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting.

Their office does not protect them from judgment.

Samuel, meanwhile, ministers before the LORD as a boy wearing a linen ephod. Hannah makes him a little robe each year. The domestic detail is tender: giving Samuel to God's service does not erase his mother's love.

A man of God announces judgment on Eli's house. Eli himself has rebuked his sons, but God says he has honored his sons above the LORD by allowing the abuse to continue.

The judgment includes a promise: God will raise up “a faithful priest” who will do what is in His heart.

The immediate historical fulfillment is connected with the later removal of Eli's priestly line and establishment of a faithful priestly house. Yet the language also participates in the Bible's larger expectation of faithful priesthood.

First Samuel therefore begins with two households: a barren woman through whom God brings life and a prestigious priestly family collapsing through corruption.

God's kingdom does not move forward according to visible status. He raises the lowly and brings down the proud.
difficult:
Hannah's vow is voluntary and tied to Samuel's special dedication. It is not a command that Christian parents bargain with God for children or surrender children to religious service.

The statement that Eli's sons “did not know the LORD” shows that holding religious office is not the same as faith.

Hannah's reference to God's king and anointed one appears before Israel's monarchy. It anticipates the royal theme that will dominate Samuel rather than proving Hannah had a fully developed later messianic understanding.
connections:
Mary's Magnificat in Luke 1 strongly echoes Hannah's song: God brings down the proud and lifts the lowly. The birth of Jesus stands in the same great biblical pattern of divine reversal.

Samuel's miraculous birth also joins a line of births in which God gives life where human ability has failed.

The contrast between corrupt priests and God's promised faithful priest ultimately finds its fullest resolution in Christ, the faithful High Priest who does not exploit worshipers but gives Himself for them.

title: Speak, LORD: Samuel Is Called and the Ark Is Captured
explanation:
Chapter 3 opens with spiritual scarcity: “The word of the LORD was rare in those days; visions were not widespread.”

Eli is old, his eyesight is failing, and the priestly house is under judgment. Yet “the lamp of God had not yet gone out.” Literally this refers to the sanctuary lamp, but in the narrative it also fits the moment: darkness has not had the final word.

Samuel hears his name and assumes Eli is calling. Three times he runs to Eli. Finally Eli understands that the LORD is calling the boy and instructs him to answer, “Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening.”

God's first message to Samuel is not pleasant. He confirms judgment on Eli's household because Eli knew of his sons' blasphemous conduct and failed to restrain them adequately.

Samuel is afraid to tell Eli, but Eli insists. Samuel tells him everything.

The chapter closes by saying the LORD was with Samuel and “did not let any of his words fall to the ground.” From Dan to Beersheba, Israel recognizes Samuel as a prophet.

Chapter 4 then shows Israel trying to use a holy object without listening to the God who speaks.

After the Philistines defeat Israel, the elders ask why the LORD allowed it. That is the right question—but instead of repentance or seeking God's word through Samuel, they decide to bring the ark of the covenant into battle: “Then it will go with us and save us.”

The grammar is revealing. The ark has become an “it” expected to guarantee victory.

Hophni and Phinehas accompany it. The Israelites shout so loudly the ground shakes. Even the Philistines are terrified because they have heard what Israel's God did in Egypt.

But Israel loses again. Thirty thousand foot soldiers die, Hophni and Phinehas are killed, and the ark is captured.

When Eli hears that the ark has been taken, he falls backward, breaks his neck, and dies. Phinehas's wife goes into labor and names her son Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel.”

Yet the next chapter shows that God's glory has not been captured.

The Philistines place the ark in the temple of Dagon at Ashdod, apparently displaying Israel's God as a defeated deity beneath Dagon.

The next morning Dagon has fallen facedown before the ark.

They stand Dagon back up.

The following morning he has fallen again, this time with head and hands broken off.

The satire is sharp: Dagon's worshipers must rescue their god from the floor, while the supposedly captured LORD needs no Israelite army to defend Him.

God's hand then falls heavily on Ashdod with tumors and devastation. The ark is moved to Gath and then Ekron, spreading panic.

The theological reversal is complete. Israel thought possessing the ark meant possessing God. The Philistines thought possessing the ark meant defeating God.

Both are wrong.

God's presence is gift, not magic. He cannot be manipulated by Israel's religious machinery, and He cannot be imprisoned by Philistine power.
difficult:
“Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening” describes Samuel's prophetic call. Christians should not assume that quieting themselves will produce an audible private revelation. God has promised to address His church through His revealed Word.

The ark was genuinely holy, but holiness did not make it a talisman. Israel's error was treating God's covenant presence as something they could control while ignoring His Word.

The precise medical identity of the Philistine “tumors” is uncertain. Some translations and ancient traditions connect them with a plague involving rodents, but the text's theological point is God's judgment, not a diagnosis.
connections:
John's Gospel says the Word became flesh and “dwelt” among us. God's presence reaches its climax not in a sacred box that humans can manipulate, but in Christ Himself.

Samuel's willingness to speak an unwelcome word is part of faithful prophetic ministry: God's messenger does not own the message.

Dagon falling before the ark anticipates the biblical conviction that idols cannot stand before the living God. The gospel does not need human manipulation to make God's Word powerful.

title: The Ark Returns and Israel Returns to the LORD
explanation:
After seven months of plague, the Philistines decide the ark must go back to Israel. Their priests and diviners advise them not to send it empty but to include a guilt offering—gold models of the tumors and mice associated with the devastation.

Their reasoning explicitly remembers Egypt: “Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?”

Israel's Exodus has become international memory.

The Philistines devise a test. They hitch two milk cows that have never worn a yoke to a cart, shut their calves away, place the ark on the cart, and let the cows go.

Normally the cows would be expected to return toward their calves. Instead they walk straight toward Beth-shemesh, lowing as they go but not turning aside.

The Philistine rulers follow and conclude that Israel's God has indeed caused their calamity.

At Beth-shemesh the Israelites rejoice, split the cart for firewood, and offer the cows as sacrifices.

Then the mood changes abruptly. Some inhabitants look into—or, depending on a textual question, look upon—the ark improperly, and God strikes them.

The Hebrew text has difficulties regarding both the exact offense and the number killed, and ancient manuscripts preserve variations. What is clear is the theological point: the ark is not less holy when it returns to Israel than when it devastates Philistia.

The people cry, “Who is able to stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?”

That is one of Samuel's central questions.

The ark is taken to Kiriath-jearim and remains there for many years.

Chapter 7 then shifts from the ark to Israel's heart. Samuel tells the people that if they are returning to the LORD wholeheartedly, they must remove the Baals and Ashtoreths and worship the LORD alone.

They do.

Israel gathers at Mizpah, fasts, confesses, “We have sinned against the LORD,” and asks Samuel to cry out to God for them.

As Samuel offers a lamb, the Philistines attack.

This time Israel does not drag the ark into battle as a magical guarantee. Samuel intercedes, God thunders against the Philistines, and Israel defeats them.

The contrast with chapter 4 is deliberate. The issue was never whether Israel had the right sacred object. The issue was whether they trusted and listened to the LORD.

Samuel sets up a stone between Mizpah and Shen and names it Ebenezer—“stone of help”—saying, “The LORD has helped us to this point.”

The name is often used sentimentally, but in context it marks a concrete deliverance after repentance and intercession.

Israel regains towns previously lost to the Philistines, and the land has a measure of peace.

Samuel then judges Israel throughout his life, traveling a circuit through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah before returning to Ramah.

These chapters complete a movement from superstition to repentance. Israel once said, in effect, “Bring the ark so it will save us.” Now they say, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us.”

God is not an object to be carried into our plans.

He is the holy Lord who calls sinners away from idols and mercifully hears them.
difficult:
The textual problems in 1 Samuel 6:19 are real. Manuscripts differ over the number struck and the wording of the offense. We can acknowledge that uncertainty without losing the passage's clear emphasis on God's holiness.

The Philistines' test with the cows is their own method for determining whether the plague came from Israel's God; Scripture reports it without establishing such tests as a normal way to discern God's will.

Ebenezer means “stone of help.” The memorial points backward to God's actual help, not to Israel's strength.
connections:
Israel's confession and Samuel's intercession anticipate the biblical need for a mediator, though Samuel himself is only a temporary and sinful human servant.

The sacrificial lamb and intercession naturally point Christian readers toward Christ, who is both sacrifice and intercessor.

The movement from idols to the LORD also illustrates repentance properly understood: not a meritorious work that earns rescue, but God's Word exposing false gods and drawing His people back to the One who saves.

title: Israel Asks for a King—and Saul Is Anointed
explanation:
Chapter 8 marks one of Israel's great transitions. Samuel is old, and his sons Joel and Abijah serve as judges in Beersheba. Like Eli's sons before them, they are corrupt: they take bribes and pervert justice.

Israel's elders therefore have a legitimate problem. But their proposed solution reveals a deeper desire: “Appoint a king to judge us the same as all the other nations have.”

Kingship itself is not inherently sinful. Deuteronomy 17 anticipated a future king and gave laws for him. The problem is Israel's motive and conception of kingship.

God tells Samuel, “They have not rejected you; they have rejected me as their king.”

Israel wants political security that looks like the surrounding nations: a king who will lead them and fight their battles.

Samuel warns them about “the rights of the king.” A king will take sons for armies and labor, daughters for service, fields and vineyards, servants and livestock. The repeated verb is “take.”

At the Exodus, God delivered Israel from a king who took. Now Israel asks for another powerful human ruler.

Still, God tells Samuel to listen to them and appoint a king.

That tension runs through the monarchy: Israel's request contains unbelief, yet God will work through kingship and eventually attach extraordinary promises to David's line.

Chapter 9 introduces Saul with impressive outward qualifications. He is a handsome young man and a head taller than everyone else.

He begins not by seeking a throne but by looking for his father's lost donkeys.

Providence quietly directs him toward Samuel. The servant happens to know that a “man of God” is nearby, they have a small gift to offer, and Samuel has already been told by God that a Benjamite will arrive.

Before Saul appears, God says, “You will anoint him ruler over my people Israel. He will save them from the Philistines, because I have seen the affliction of my people, for their cry has come to me.”

That statement is gracious. Even though Israel's demand for a king expresses rejection, God hears their distress.

Samuel privately anoints Saul and kisses him.

Chapter 10 gives Saul confirming signs. He will meet men who tell him the donkeys are found, receive bread from travelers, and encounter a group of prophets. The Spirit of the LORD will come powerfully on him, and he will prophesy.

Everything occurs as Samuel said.

The Spirit's empowerment here equips Saul for royal service. It should not automatically be equated with the New Testament's full teaching about regeneration or the permanent indwelling of the Spirit.

Samuel then gathers Israel and again reminds them that their demand for a king has involved rejecting the God who saved them.

The lot identifies Saul—but Saul is hiding among the supplies.

His height is impressive; his confidence is not.

When he is brought out, Samuel says, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among the entire population.”

The people shout, “Long live the king!”

Yet some men despise him and ask how he can save them. Saul remains silent.

These chapters intentionally leave us with mixed signals. Saul is truly chosen and anointed by God. He receives the Spirit and is given signs. God intends to use him.

At the same time, the people's desire for visible human security is spiritually dangerous, and Saul's impressive appearance will soon prove an unreliable measure of kingship.

First Samuel is preparing us to ask: what kind of king does God's people actually need?
difficult:
Israel's request for a king is sinful in motive but kingship itself is not condemned. Deuteronomy anticipated a king, and God will later establish the Davidic covenant.

The Spirit coming on Saul is empowerment for his calling. Old Testament descriptions of the Spirit's coming and departing should not simply be mapped onto New Testament language about baptism and regeneration.

Saul's selection by lot occurs within Israel's particular covenant setting. It is not a general method Christians are commanded to use for selecting leaders.
connections:
Samuel's warning about a king who “takes” creates a contrast with God's own kingship and eventually with Jesus, the King who comes not to be served but to serve and give His life.

God hears Israel's cry even while correcting the unbelief mixed into their request. His mercy is greater than the purity of their motives.

Saul's outward impressiveness also prepares for David's anointing, when God explicitly tells Samuel that humans look at outward appearance but the LORD looks at the heart.

title: Saul's Victory and Samuel's Covenant Farewell
explanation:
Saul's public kingship begins with a genuine act of deliverance.

Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead. When the people ask for terms, Nahash offers a deliberately humiliating condition: he will gouge out every man's right eye “and bring disgrace on all Israel.”

The threat is both brutal and political. Mutilation would mark Israel's humiliation and could impair warriors who used shields in battle.

The people send messengers throughout Israel. When Saul hears, “the Spirit of God came powerfully on him,” and he burns with anger.

This anger is not presented as petty rage. It responds to violent oppression.

Saul cuts up oxen and sends the pieces throughout Israel, warning those who refuse to follow. The fear of the LORD falls on the people, and they gather as one.

Saul divides the army, attacks the Ammonites at dawn, and wins decisively.

Afterward some Israelites want to execute those who had previously despised Saul. Saul refuses: “No one will be executed this day, for today the LORD has provided deliverance in Israel.”

This is Saul at his best. He gives God credit for victory and refuses to use success to settle personal scores.

The kingdom is then renewed at Gilgal, where Saul is confirmed before the LORD with sacrifices and rejoicing.

Chapter 12 functions as Samuel's public farewell from national leadership, though he will continue as prophet.

He invites Israel to testify against him: whose ox has he taken? Whom has he cheated? From whom has he accepted a bribe?

The people acknowledge his integrity.

This is especially significant after Samuel's warning in chapter 8 about kings who “take.” Samuel's leadership has not been based on enriching himself.

He then rehearses Israel's history. God sent Moses and Aaron, delivered Israel from Egypt, and repeatedly raised deliverers when Israel cried out.

The pattern is familiar from Judges: Israel forgets; enemies oppress; Israel confesses; God saves.

Then Samuel identifies the request for a king as another act of distrust, especially because the LORD was already their king.

To confirm the seriousness of their sin, Samuel calls on God to send thunder and rain during the wheat harvest, when such weather would be unusual and damaging. God does so, and the people fear.

They ask Samuel to pray that they will not die, admitting they have added the evil of asking for a king to their other sins.

Samuel's answer is one of the most important grace statements in the book:

“Don't be afraid. Even though you have committed all this evil, don't turn away from following the LORD.”

Israel's sin is named plainly. Grace does not require pretending the sin was minor.

But Samuel continues: “The LORD will not abandon his people, because of his great name and because he has determined to make you his own people.”

The foundation is God's name and God's determination, not Israel's ability to repair its record.

Samuel also says it would be a sin for him to stop praying for them. He will continue teaching them “the good and right way.”

The chapter ends with both promise and warning. Israel and its king must fear and serve the LORD. Persistent rebellion will bring judgment.

The monarchy has begun, but nothing fundamental has changed about who Israel's true King is.

Saul may sit on a throne.

The LORD still saves.
difficult:
Saul's anger in chapter 11 is associated with the Spirit and directed against violent injustice. That does not make every intense anger righteous; Scripture elsewhere warns how easily human anger becomes sinful.

Samuel's thunderstorm is a prophetic sign specifically given in Israel's covenant setting, not a pattern for demanding miraculous weather as confirmation.

God's promise not to abandon Israel “because of his great name” does not eliminate covenant warnings. The chapter holds divine faithfulness and serious judgment together.
connections:
Samuel's refusal to exploit his office offers a biblical standard for spiritual leadership: authority is not permission for self-enrichment.

His continuing intercession points toward Christ, who perfectly intercedes for His people.

Most importantly, God's commitment rests on His own name. Lutheran theology rightly emphasizes this direction of salvation: our hope rests not on the strength of our promise to God but on the faithfulness of God's promise to us.

title: Saul's Unraveling: Sacrifice, Rashness, and Rejected Kingship
explanation:
These chapters trace Saul's rapid decline.

Chapter 13 opens with textual difficulty: the Hebrew text preserving Saul's age and length of reign is damaged, which is why translations differ or include footnotes. The narrative itself quickly moves to war with the Philistines.

Jonathan attacks a Philistine outpost, and the Philistines gather an enormous force. Israelites hide in caves, holes, and cisterns.

Saul waits at Gilgal for Samuel, but as his troops scatter he offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives immediately afterward.

Saul explains that Samuel was late, the army was leaving, the Philistines were gathering, and he had not yet “sought the LORD's favor,” so he “forced” himself to sacrifice.

His reasoning sounds practical. But Samuel says he has acted foolishly by not keeping God's command. His dynasty will not endure; God will seek “a man after his own heart.”

The issue is not simply that Saul performed a ritual reserved for priests; kings sometimes participated in sacrificial contexts. The narrative emphasizes his refusal to wait for the prophetic word and his attempt to secure God's favor on his own timetable.

Chapter 14 contrasts Saul with Jonathan.

Jonathan and his armor-bearer approach a Philistine outpost trusting that “nothing can keep the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.”

God sends panic, and Israel begins winning.

Saul, however, makes a rash oath: no one may eat until he has taken vengeance on his enemies. The exhausted troops become weaker.

Jonathan has not heard the oath and eats honey. His eyes brighten, and he correctly observes that his father has troubled the land.

Worse, starving soldiers later slaughter animals and eat meat with blood, violating God's law. Saul's supposedly zealous command has contributed to actual disobedience.

When the lot identifies Jonathan as the oath-breaker, Saul is prepared to execute his own son despite Jonathan's role in the victory. The people intervene: “As the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground.”

The king who should protect Israel must be restrained by Israel from killing its deliverer.

Chapter 15 is decisive.

God commands Saul through Samuel to place Amalek under *herem*—the conquest judgment associated with Amalek's earlier attack on vulnerable Israelites.

The moral difficulty is substantial. The command includes comprehensive destruction. The text locates this within a particular divine judgment in Israel's covenant history; it is not a standing mandate for God's people to destroy religious or ethnic enemies.

Saul defeats Amalek but spares King Agag and the best livestock.

When Samuel confronts him, Saul initially insists, “I have carried out the LORD's instructions.”

Then sheep bleat in the background.

Saul blames the people and claims the animals were spared to sacrifice to God.

Samuel answers with the famous principle: “To obey is better than sacrifice.”

God cannot be bribed with religious activity into accepting disobedience. Worship offered as a substitute for listening to God's Word becomes rebellion.

Saul finally admits sin but immediately adds that he feared the people. He then begs Samuel to honor him before Israel's elders.

His concern for public standing remains painfully visible.

Samuel announces that God has torn the kingdom from Saul and given it to someone better.

The chapter says God “regretted” making Saul king, while also saying the Glory of Israel “does not lie or change his mind, for he is not a man that he should change his mind.”

Those statements are intentionally close together. God's “regret” describes His real grief and changed dealings with Saul within history; it does not mean God discovered a mistake or acquired information He lacked.

Saul was truly chosen, truly empowered, and truly given a vocation.

His fall is not because God's Word failed.

It is because Saul increasingly treats God's Word as something to manage around his own fear, timing, reputation, and religious reasoning.
difficult:
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 13:1 is corrupt or incomplete, producing translation differences regarding Saul's age and reign. Acts 13:21 supplies a forty-year reign tradition.

The Amalek command is among Scripture's hardest judgment texts. It must remain a unique divine judgment, not a model for Christian violence or ethnic hostility.

God's “regret” in 15:11 and 15:35 should be read alongside 15:29. Scripture can speak of God's genuine relational grief and changed historical action while also denying that He is fickle or mistaken like a human being.
connections:
“To obey is better than sacrifice” is not an attack on the sacrificial system God Himself instituted. It attacks the attempt to use worship to cover rebellion.

Saul's need to preserve his honor before people contrasts with the later Son of David, who accepts shame in obedience to His Father.

The “man after God's own heart” prepares for David, but David too will sin grievously. Ultimately the faithful King Israel needs is greater than either Saul or David.

title: David Anointed and Goliath Defeated
explanation:
Samuel grieves over Saul, but God tells him to go to Bethlehem and anoint one of Jesse's sons.

Samuel sees Eliab and immediately thinks, “Certainly the LORD's anointed one is here before him.”

Eliab apparently looks kingly.

God corrects Samuel: “Do not look at his appearance or his stature... Humans do not see what the LORD sees, for humans see what is visible, but the LORD sees the heart.”

The contrast with Saul is deliberate. Saul was introduced as exceptionally handsome and taller than everyone. God is now teaching Samuel not to choose by the same visible standards.

Seven sons pass before Samuel, but none is chosen. The youngest, David, is out keeping sheep and is not even initially invited to the sacrifice.

When David arrives, God says, “Anoint him.”

Samuel pours oil on him, and “the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on David from that day forward.”

The next verse says the Spirit departed from Saul and “an evil spirit from the LORD” terrified him.

This is difficult language. The text affirms God's sovereignty even over the spirit that troubles Saul; it does not require us to conclude that God morally turns Saul evil. Nor should we confidently diagnose Saul with a modern psychiatric condition from an ancient theological narrative.

David enters Saul's service as a skilled musician, and his playing brings Saul relief.

Chapter 17 tells the famous confrontation with Goliath.

Goliath is a massive Philistine champion from Gath, heavily armored and armed. His challenge turns battle into representative combat: send one man; the winner's people will dominate the loser's.

For forty days Israel hears his defiance and is terrified.

David arrives to bring food to his brothers and hears Goliath mocking “the armies of the living God.”

His perspective differs from everyone else's. Saul and the soldiers measure David against Goliath. David measures Goliath against the LORD.

David refuses Saul's armor because he has not tested it. Instead he takes his staff, sling, and five smooth stones.

His speech is the theological center: “You come against me with a sword, spear, and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Armies.”

He continues: the battle is the LORD's.

David kills Goliath with a sling stone, then uses Goliath's own sword to cut off his head. The Philistine army flees.

This story is often reduced to “face your giants.” That misses its center.

Israel does not defeat Goliath because every Israelite discovers the courage to fight his personal giant. Israel stands helpless while an anointed representative goes out on their behalf and wins a victory they could not win themselves.

David's faith is genuine and exemplary, but the structure is representative deliverance.

There is also a textual issue surrounding David's introduction to Saul. Chapter 16 says David served Saul as musician and armor-bearer, while 17:55–58 depicts Saul asking whose son David is.

Various explanations are possible: Saul may be asking specifically about David's family because victory brings royal privileges; the stories may preserve distinct narrative traditions; or David's earlier service may have been intermittent and not personally memorable to Saul. The text does not resolve every detail for us.

What it makes unmistakable is that God's chosen king emerges from obscurity, not outward impressiveness, and delivers Israel through trust in the LORD rather than conventional power.
difficult:
The “evil spirit from the LORD” should not be used to diagnose Saul medically or to say God is morally evil. The biblical writer is emphasizing God's sovereignty over Saul's judgment and distress.

Goliath's exact height differs in textual traditions. The traditional Hebrew text gives “six cubits and a span,” while the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint tradition support “four cubits and a span.” Either reading describes a formidable warrior.

The apparent tension between chapters 16 and 17 regarding Saul's knowledge of David is real and has several plausible explanations; certainty is unwarranted.
connections:
David's victory naturally points beyond moral encouragement toward representative salvation: the anointed king fights while Israel watches and receives the benefit.

That pattern reaches its fulfillment in the Son of David. Christ defeats sin, death, and the devil not by inspiring us first to win the battle ourselves, but by winning for us.

Only then does Christian courage follow from a victory already given.

title: Saul's Jealousy and Jonathan's Covenant Loyalty
explanation:
After Goliath's defeat, David's rise accelerates—and Saul's fear of him grows.

Jonathan, Saul's son and expected heir, forms a covenant with David and gives him his robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt. Whatever precise political symbolism is intended, Jonathan's actions are remarkable. He does not treat David merely as a rival for his future throne.

David succeeds wherever Saul sends him.

When women celebrate the returning army—“Saul has killed his thousands, but David his tens of thousands”—Saul becomes furious. The song need not mean David literally deserves ten times more credit; Hebrew poetry often uses escalating numbers for rhetorical effect. Saul hears it as a threat to his status.

“From that day on Saul kept watching David jealously.”

The next day Saul hurls a spear at David while David plays music. David escapes.

Saul is afraid because “the LORD was with David but had left Saul.”

That is the tragic reversal. Saul's central concern becomes preserving the kingship God has already said will not remain with his house.

He tries to use his daughters as bait. He first offers Merab and then Michal, hoping David will die fighting Philistines. David cannot afford the normal bride-price, so Saul demands a grisly military price—one hundred Philistine foreskins.

David doubles it and survives.

Michal loves David, Jonathan loves David, Israel favors David, and God is with David. Every attempt Saul makes to eliminate him only increases David's standing.

Chapter 19 escalates from secret plots to an open command that Jonathan and Saul's servants kill David.

Jonathan warns David and then reasons with his father. He reminds Saul that David has served him well and risked his life against Goliath. Saul temporarily swears David will not die.

But after another military success, Saul again tries to spear David.

Michal helps David escape through a window and uses a household idol, a *teraphim*, to make it appear he is in bed. The presence of such an object in Saul's household is another unsettling glimpse of Israel's mixed religious life.

David flees to Samuel at Ramah. Saul sends groups to seize him, but God's Spirit overwhelms the messengers and they prophesy. Finally Saul himself comes and is overcome in the same way.

The king's attempt to control God's anointed is rendered powerless by God's Spirit.

Chapter 20 centers on Jonathan.

David believes Saul intends to kill him; Jonathan initially struggles to believe his father would hide such a plan from him. They devise a test involving the new-moon feast.

Saul's response confirms the danger. When Jonathan defends David, Saul insults his own son and throws a spear at him too.

Jonathan now understands that Saul's obsession threatens even his family.

Jonathan and David renew their covenant. Jonathan asks David to show steadfast love not only to him but to his house when God removes David's enemies.

That request becomes important later when David shows kindness to Jonathan's son Mephibosheth.

The friends separate in grief.

These chapters contrast two responses to God's choice. Saul sees David's rise and clings desperately to power. Jonathan sees the same reality and responds with covenant loyalty, even though it costs him his own expected succession.

Jonathan's greatness lies partly in his willingness not to make himself the center of God's story.
difficult:
The recurring troubling spirit language continues the judgment theme from chapter 16 and should not be converted into a modern medical diagnosis.

Michal's use of a household idol does not imply the narrator approves possession of *teraphim*. It shows how religiously compromised even important Israelite households could be.

Jonathan's covenant with David includes political implications, but it is also deeply personal. Attempts to reduce their relationship either to pure political calculation or to a modern sexual category go beyond the text.
connections:
Jonathan's willingness to yield status rather than fight God's chosen king offers a striking contrast with Saul's grasping.

David remains God's anointed while living as a hunted fugitive. God's promise can be true even when circumstances look opposite to fulfillment.

The New Testament's Son of David will likewise be rejected before enthronement. Yet unlike David, Jesus' path to kingship passes through a cross for His enemies as well as His friends.

title: David the Fugitive and the Massacre of the Priests
explanation:
David is now a fugitive from the king he faithfully served.

He goes to Ahimelech the priest at Nob and lies, claiming Saul has sent him on a secret mission. David asks for food, and the only bread available is the consecrated bread that had been before the LORD.

Ahimelech gives it after asking about ritual purity.

Jesus later refers to this episode when His disciples are criticized for plucking grain on the Sabbath. His point is not that God's commands are meaningless whenever someone is hungry. He appeals to a biblical precedent showing that ceremonial regulations are not rightly interpreted in a way that ignores mercy and human need.

David also asks for a weapon and receives Goliath's sword.

One ominous detail appears: Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul's officials, is present and sees what happens.

David then flees to Achish king of Gath—the hometown of Goliath, whose sword David is carrying. Philistine servants recognize him and repeat the song about David's victories.

David becomes afraid and pretends to be insane, scratching doors and letting saliva run down his beard.

Achish dismisses him with dark humor: “Do I have such a shortage of crazy people that you brought this one to act crazy around me?”

David escapes to the cave of Adullam.

There his family joins him, along with about four hundred men described as distressed, indebted, or bitter. The future king's first following is not the social elite. It is a collection of desperate people.

David arranges protection for his parents with the king of Moab. Ruth's Moabite ancestry may form part of the background to that connection, though the text does not say so explicitly.

Chapter 22 returns to Saul.

Saul sits with spear in hand, accusing his own Benjamite officials of conspiring with David. He complains that no one feels sorry for him.

The king who once appeared humble is now consumed by self-pity and suspicion.

Doeg tells Saul that he saw David with Ahimelech.

Saul summons Ahimelech and the priests. Ahimelech truthfully explains that David was Saul's trusted servant and son-in-law and that he knew nothing of rebellion.

Saul orders the priests killed.

His own guards refuse.

Doeg obeys.

He kills eighty-five priests and then attacks Nob, slaughtering men, women, children, infants, and animals.

The horror is deliberate. Saul had failed to carry out God's judgment against Amalek in chapter 15; now he carries out comprehensive destruction against the LORD's own priestly town.

One priest, Abiathar, escapes to David.

David immediately recognizes his responsibility: he knew Doeg was present and suspected he would tell Saul. “I am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father's family.”

David's deception at Nob therefore has consequences. Scripture does not sanitize him simply because he is the chosen king.

Yet David tells Abiathar to remain with him: “The one who wants to take my life wants to take your life. You will be safe with me.”

The contrast with Saul is stark.

People near Saul die because the king is trying to preserve himself.

A hunted priest finds refuge with David.

Still, David is not yet the perfect king. His fear, deception, and choices have contributed to tragedy.

The story is teaching us to hope in God's promise without turning God's chosen servants into flawless heroes.
difficult:
David lies to Ahimelech and later acknowledges his role in the resulting disaster. The narrative does not require us to call the deception righteous simply because David is God's anointed.

Jesus' use of the consecrated bread episode in the Gospels emphasizes mercy and the proper interpretation of sacred law; it does not erase all boundaries around holy things.

Saul's massacre of Nob is his own wicked act. The earlier prophecy of judgment on Eli's house forms part of the larger narrative background, but divine judgment does not make Saul or Doeg morally innocent.
connections:
Jesus explicitly invokes David eating the consecrated bread, placing this obscure fugitive episode within His teaching about Sabbath and mercy.

David's gathering of distressed and indebted followers faintly anticipates the way God's kingdom often gathers those without worldly status.

But the contrast is also necessary: David's failures contribute to others' suffering; Christ, the greater Son of David, bears others' guilt and suffering Himself.

title: David Spares Saul—and Abigail Stops a Foolish Revenge
explanation:
David's fugitive years continue, but these chapters show God preserving him while also restraining him from becoming like Saul.

Chapter 23 begins when David hears that Philistines are attacking Keilah. His own men are afraid, but David inquires of the LORD and is told to go.

He rescues the town.

Then Saul hears David is inside a walled city and concludes, remarkably, “God has handed him over to me.”

Saul can still use religious language while pursuing the man God has chosen.

David again seeks God's guidance and learns that Keilah's leaders will surrender him to Saul. He leaves.

Jonathan then finds David in the wilderness and “strengthened his hand in God.” He tells David not to fear and openly acknowledges, “You yourself will be king over Israel, and I'll be your second-in-command.”

This is Jonathan's final recorded meeting with David.

The Ziphites betray David's location, and Saul nearly traps him, but a Philistine invasion forces Saul to break off pursuit.

Chapter 24 creates the opportunity David's men have been waiting for. Saul enters a cave to relieve himself, unaware that David and his men are hiding farther inside.

David's men interpret the opportunity providentially: this must be the day God promised to give Saul into David's hand.

David creeps forward and cuts off the corner of Saul's robe.

Then his conscience strikes him.

He refuses to kill “the LORD's anointed.”

David's restraint does not mean Saul's behavior is acceptable or that an abusive ruler must never be resisted. David has already fled, protected himself, and will continue avoiding Saul. His point is that he will not seize the throne through private murder of the king God installed.

Outside the cave David proves that he could have killed Saul. Saul weeps, admits David is more righteous, and acknowledges that David will become king.

Yet David wisely does not return to Saul's court.

Forgiveness or refusal to retaliate does not require pretending a dangerous person has become trustworthy.

Chapter 25 begins with Samuel's death and then introduces Nabal and Abigail.

David's men have protected Nabal's shepherds and flocks in the wilderness. During shearing—a festive time—David asks for provisions.

Nabal contemptuously replies, “Who is David? Who is Jesse's son?” and refuses.

David reacts badly. He straps on his sword and vows to kill every male in Nabal's household.

The man who spared Saul is now prepared to massacre a household because he has been insulted.

Abigail intervenes.

She quickly gathers generous provisions, meets David, bows, and delivers one of the wisest speeches in Samuel.

She asks David not to take bloodguilt on himself by avenging his own cause. God is building David “a lasting dynasty”; therefore David should not arrive at kingship burdened by needless bloodshed and personal revenge.

Her argument calls David back to God's promise.

If God has promised the throne, David does not need to secure his honor through vengeance.

David recognizes this immediately: “Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today!”

He even blesses Abigail's discernment for preventing him from bloodguilt.

Nabal later dies after the LORD strikes him. David did not need to take vengeance into his own hands.

David then marries Abigail.

These chapters contain an important pattern. David sometimes restrains himself, and sometimes he needs someone else to restrain him.

God's providence preserves David not only from Saul but also from David's own anger.
difficult:
David's refusal to kill Saul should not be turned into a blanket command that Christians remain physically present under abusive authority. David repeatedly escapes Saul and takes protective action.

Nabal's refusal of hospitality occurs in a culture where David's men had materially protected his shepherds. Even so, Nabal's insult does not justify David's intended massacre.

Abigail's intervention is portrayed as wise and faithful even though she acts without first obtaining her husband's permission. The narrative praises her for preventing bloodshed.
connections:
Jonathan strengthens David “in God,” not merely by telling him to believe in himself. Biblical encouragement directs faith toward God's promise.

Abigail's argument against personal vengeance resonates strongly with later biblical teaching: vengeance belongs to God.
